李華春〔貫福建泉州府晉江縣民籍，浙江崇德縣人，國子生，治易經，字君實，行一，年三十二，十月二十日生〕。曾祖開先，祖茂，父伯剛，前母高氏，母殷氏。永感下，兄榮春，弟貴春、棉春、任春、頃、逢春、陽春，娶許氏。福建鄉試第二名，會試第三百十九名。

苗淳然〔貫直隸廣平府曲周縣民籍，府學附學生，治詩經，字秀卿，行一，年二十八，正月初一日生〕。曾祖富，祖子用，父虎，母陳氏。慈侍下，弟油然、沛然、滋然，娶李氏。順天府鄉試第二十三名，會試第三百六十八名。

彭應時〔貫江西吉安府廬陵縣民籍，府學附學生，治詩經，字化中，行一，年三十一，三月十八日生〕。曾祖宣傑，祖徽名，父造越，母蕭氏。慈侍下，兄應春，弟應曉，娶蕭氏。江西鄉試第三十九名，會試第二百四十三名。

王學書〔貫山東濟南府濱州軍籍，國子生，治書經，字惟中，行三，年三十八，十二月初七日生〕。曾祖勝，祖山，父允，母汪氏。永感下，兄汝登、汝科，弟學詩、學禮、學易、學顏、學曾，娶于氏，繼娶鄭氏。山東鄉試第七十名，會試第九十八名。
translation_en:
Li Huachun, courtesy name Junshi, was registered in a civilian household in Jinjiang County, Quanzhou Prefecture, Fujian, and was a native of Chongde County, Zhejiang; he was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Changes, ranked first in birth order, and was thirty-two years old, born on the twentieth day of the tenth month. His great-grandfather was Kaixian, his grandfather Mao, and his father Bogang; his father's former wife was née Gao and his mother née Yin; both parents were deceased; his elder brother was Rongchun and his younger brothers were Guichun, Mianchun, Renchun, Qing [?], Fengchun, and Yangchun; his wife was née Xu; he placed second in the Fujian Provincial Examination and 319th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Miao Chunran, courtesy name Xiuqing, was registered in a civilian household in Quzhou County, Guangping Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region; he was an additional student of the prefectural school specializing in the Book of Odes, ranked first in birth order, and was twenty-eight years old, born on the first day of the first month. His great-grandfather was Fu, his grandfather Ziyong, and his father Hu; his mother was née Chen; his father was deceased and his mother living; his younger brothers were Youran, Peiran, and Ziran; his wife was née Li; he placed twenty-third in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 368th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Peng Yingshi, courtesy name Huazhong, was registered in a civilian household in Luling County, Ji'an Prefecture, Jiangxi; he was an additional student of the prefectural school specializing in the Book of Odes, ranked first in birth order, and was thirty-one years old, born on the eighteenth day of the third month. His great-grandfather was Xuanjie, his grandfather Huiming, and his father Zaoyue; his mother was née Xiao; his father was deceased and his mother living; his elder brother was Yingchun and his younger brother Yingxiao; his wife was née Xiao; he placed thirty-ninth in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and 243rd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Xueshu, courtesy name Weizhong, was registered in a military household in Binzhou, Jinan Prefecture, Shandong; he was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Documents, ranked third in birth order, and was thirty-eight years old, born on the seventh day of the twelfth month. His great-grandfather was Sheng, his grandfather Shan, and his father Yun; his mother was née Wang; both parents were deceased; his elder brothers were Rudeng and Ruke, and his younger brothers Xueshi, Xueli, Xueyi, Xueyan, and Xuezeng; his wife was née Yu, and he subsequently married a woman née Zheng; he placed seventieth in the Shandong Provincial Examination and ninety-eighth in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Liu Yucheng, registered in a civilian household in Changzhou County, Suzhou Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, was a native of Taicang Subprefecture and a supplementary student of the county school. He specialized in the Book of Changes; his courtesy name was Zifu, he ranked first among his brothers, and he was aged thirty-two, born on the fourteenth day of the second lunar month. His great-grandfather was Wenbei, his grandfather Kun, his father Zhiliang, and his mother née You. His mother was living and his father deceased. His younger brothers were Yuzhen and Yujie, and his wife was née Zhou. He placed 113th in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and seventy-fourth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Cao Gao was registered in a civilian household in Xiuning County, Huizhou Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, and was a supplementary student of the county school. He specialized in the Book of Changes; his courtesy name was Zhongxuan, he ranked third among his brothers, and he was aged thirty-one, born on the eleventh day of the ninth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Gui, a county magistrate; his grandfather was Xianzheng, his father Xian, and his mother née Jin. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Jinglun and Jingji, his younger brothers Jingguo and Jingde, and his wife was née Jin. He placed 126th in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and forty-eighth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Sun Mingfeng was registered in a civilian household in Gao'an County, Ruizhou Prefecture, Jiangxi, and was a supplementary student of the prefectural school. He specialized in the Book of Changes; his courtesy name was Wenrui, he ranked ninth among his brothers, and he was aged twenty-seven, born on the eighth day of the tenth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Zixing, his grandfather Hongdao, his father Keju, and his mother née Yang. Both parents were living. His younger brother was Mingluan, and his wife was née Yi. He placed fifty-ninth in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and ninety-fourth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Chen Lü was registered in a salt-producing household in Dongguan County, Guangzhou Prefecture, Guangdong, and was a student of the National University. He specialized in the Book of Changes; his courtesy name was Deji, he ranked first among his brothers, and he was aged thirty-eight, born on the sixth day of the twelfth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Jin; his grandfather was Zhijing, a vice prefect; his father was Tingdui, his mother née Deng, and his stepmother née Cai. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Fu, Yi, Jing, and Yu, and his wife was née Fang. He placed thirty-sixth in the Guangdong Provincial Examination and 242nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Wang Ting 王莛, courtesy name Zicai, was registered in a civilian household in Shangcheng County, Guang Prefecture, Runing Prefecture, Henan. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Classic of Poetry, he ranked first among his brothers and was forty-six years old, born on the twenty-first day of the second month. His great-grandfather was Hui; his grandfather, Ming, was honorifically appointed Gentleman for Receiving Virtue and Secretary in the Ministry of Revenue; his father, Zhe, was a Surveillance Vice Commissioner; and his mother, née Zeng, was granted the title Lady of Repose. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Huai, Shi, Cong, Zi (a tribute scholar), and Ba. His wife was née Li. He placed eleventh in the Henan Provincial Examination and 357th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Dong Guangyu 董光裕, courtesy name Zishun, was registered in an artisan household in Hongdong County, Pingyang Prefecture, Shanxi. A county government school student specializing in the Classic of Changes, he ranked third among his brothers and was thirty years old, born on the twenty-fifth day of the seventh month. His great-grandfather was Yue (an honorary official); his grandfather was Fu; and his father, Rulin, was a Professor in a princely establishment. His father's former wife was née Song, his mother was née Zhang, and his stepmother was née Guo. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Guangzu, Shengzu, and Jingzu; his younger brothers were Shangzu, Guangmo, Guanglie, Guangde, and Guangshi. He married a woman née Zhang and subsequently a woman née Yang. He placed sixty-second in the Shanxi Provincial Examination and 397th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Li Tianzhi 李天植, courtesy name Xingfu, was registered in a military household in Guangde Subprefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region. A subprefectural government school student specializing in the Record of Rites, he ranked second among his brothers and was thirty-five years old, born on the sixth day of the tenth month. His great-grandfather was Chang; his grandfather, Tian, was a County Magistrate; his father was Shangzhi; and his mother was née Shen. His mother was living and his father deceased. His wife was née Bu. He placed fifteenth in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 152nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Zhixiang 王致祥, courtesy name Dezheng, was registered in an officer household of Longmen Guard under the Wanquan Regional Military Commission, and his family originated in Xin Subprefecture, Shanxi. A guard school student specializing in the Spring and Autumn Annals, he ranked fourth among his brothers and was twenty-eight years old, born on the twenty-second day of the eleventh month. His great-grandfather was Yong; his grandfather, Mao, was an Assistant Instructor; his father, Jin, was a Subprefectural Vice Magistrate; and his mother was née Zhang. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Zhizhong, Guoxun (an Assistant Commander), Zhihe (a tribute student by imperial grace), and Zhidao. His wife was née Liu. He placed 111th in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 171st in the Metropolitan Examination.

袁國臣〔貫湖廣承天府潛江縣，民籍，縣學生，治書經，字惟鄰，行二，年三十六，三月二十三日生〕。曾祖寅，祖應麒，父紀，母李氏。具慶下，兄國輔，弟國相、國賓、國棟、國器，娶梁氏。湖廣鄉試第五十八名，會試第二百二十八名。
translation_en:
Wang Huan, courtesy name Kuizhang, was registered in a military household in Xianning County, Wuchang Prefecture, Huguang; he was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Documents, ranked first among his brothers, and was aged thirty-nine, born on the thirtieth day of the second lunar month. His great-grandfather was Shengjian; his grandfather, Qi, was a vice prefect; his father, Xianzhen, was a judge; and his mother was née Yu. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Yue, a student of the Directorate of Education, Lian, Tun, and Can; his wife was née Qian. He placed twenty-fifth in the Huguang Provincial Examination and eighty-fifth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Du, courtesy name Weizhen, was registered in a civilian household in Shenze County, Qizhou, Baoding Prefecture, Zhili; he was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Odes, ranked first among his brothers, and was aged thirty-six, born on the fifth day of the third lunar month. His great-grandfather was Xian, his grandfather Pu, his father Chaodong, and his mother née Cao. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Fu, Lian, and Shu; his wife was née Lü. He placed 109th in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 316th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Sang Weigao, courtesy name Ruyi, was registered in a civilian household in Yuci County, Taiyuan Prefecture, Shanxi; he was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Odes, ranked first among his brothers, and was aged thirty-nine, born on the twenty-ninth day of the sixth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Tai, who held an honorary official title for longevity; his grandfather was Yuande, his father 𣠄 (reading uncertain [?]), and his mother née Bai. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Weijie, Weizhen, Weijing, Weizhi, and Weiyi; his wife was née Wang. He placed sixteenth in the Shanxi Provincial Examination and 256th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Yuan Guochen, courtesy name Weilin, was registered in a civilian household in Qianjiang County, Chengtian Prefecture, Huguang; he was a county school student specializing in the Book of Documents, ranked second among his brothers, and was aged thirty-six, born on the twenty-third day of the third lunar month. His great-grandfather was Yin, his grandfather Yingqi, his father Ji, and his mother née Li. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Guofu, and his younger brothers were Guoxiang, Guobin, Guodong, and Guoqi; his wife was née Liang. He placed fifty-eighth in the Huguang Provincial Examination and 228th in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Wu Zhimei, courtesy name Xuezhou, was registered in a banner household of Dengzhou Guard, Shandong, and was a native of Taizhou in Zhili. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Odes, he was first in birth order, aged thirty-eight, and born on the thirteenth day of the sixth month. His great-grandfather was Zhen; his grandfather He was posthumously granted the titles Gentleman of Cultivated Learning and Judge; his father Chang was an Investigating Censor; and his mother, née Ding, was granted the title Lady (ruren). Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Zhishan, an Imperial University student, Zhiyi, and Zhidao. His wife was née Pu. He placed fifty-seventh in the Shandong Provincial Examination and 277th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Qin Shen, courtesy name Zipei, was registered in a guardsman's household of the Embroidered-uniform Guard and was a native of Jianchang County, Jiangxi. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Odes, he was fourth in birth order, aged thirty-three, and born on the nineteenth day of the second month. His great-grandfather Ming was a Battalion Commander; his grandfather was Rong; and his father Lu was an Office Supervisor in the Court of Imperial Entertainments. His mother was née Li, and his stepmother was née Wang. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Jing, Lun, and Jin. He married a woman née Deng and subsequently a woman née Chen. He placed 135th in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 330th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Bai Dong, courtesy name Zilong, was registered in a military officer household of the Right Battalion of Yulin Guard, Shaanxi, and was a native of Mizhi County. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Changes, he was first in birth order, aged forty, and born on the fourth day of the tenth month. His great-grandfather was Yongqian; his grandfather Cong was a Platoon Commander entitled to wear official cap and belt; his father Qiyou was a Battalion Commander; and his mother, née Song, was granted the title Lady of Suitability (yiren). Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Pu, Shu (术) [?], Yang, a Battalion Commander, Qiao, Yu, and Kai. His wife was née Zhu. He placed fifty-third in the Shaanxi Provincial Examination and 151st in the Metropolitan Examination.

Xue Menglei, courtesy name Rufen, was registered in a civilian household in Houguan County, Fuzhou Prefecture, Fujian, and was a native of Fuqing County. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Odes, he was second in birth order, aged twenty-six, and born on the third day of the eighth month. His great-grandfather was Chongde; his grandfather was Qingyun; his father Yicai was an official awaiting selection for appointment; and his mother was née Lin. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Menglong, a Metropolitan Examination graduate (gongshi), and Mengqi; his younger brothers were Mengliang, Menghe, Mengxiong, and Mengyue. He married a woman née Lin and subsequently a woman née Zhao. He placed thirty-first in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and ninety-third in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Shuai Lan 帥蘭, courtesy name Tongfu, was registered in a civilian household in Jiangling County, Jingzhou Prefecture, Huguang, and was a native of Jiangxia County, Wuchang Prefecture. A student of the Imperial University specializing in the Book of Odes, he was third in birth order, aged forty-one, and born on the twenty-fourth day of the seventh month. His great-grandfather was Yongrong; his grandfather, Zhonggang; and his father, Jin. His father's former wife was née Deng, and his mother was née Li. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Yi and Jin, and his younger brother was Zhi. He married a woman née Zhu and subsequently a woman née Xiao. He placed twentieth in the Huguang Provincial Examination and three hundredth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Liu Xie 劉諧, courtesy name Fenghe, was registered in a civilian household in Macheng County, Huangzhou Prefecture, Huguang. A student of the Imperial University specializing in the Spring and Autumn Annals, he was second in birth order, aged thirty-two, and born on the fourth day of the second month. His great-grandfather was Mingshan; his grandfather, Ji, posthumously granted the titles Grand Master for Governance and Bureau Director in the Ministry of Justice; and his father, Tingju, a Surveillance Vice Commissioner. His mother, née Li, was ennobled as Lady of Suitability. Both parents were living. His elder brother Qian was a student of the Imperial University; his younger brothers were Hui and Cheng. He married a woman née Wang. He placed sixteenth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and thirty-eighth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Song Fan 宋范, courtesy name Xifan, was registered in a civilian household in Yongnian County, Guangping Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region. A student of the Imperial University specializing in the Book of Odes, he was second in birth order, aged thirty-nine, and born on the twenty-second day of the ninth month. His great-grandfather was Da; his grandfather, Jie; and his father, Zizhen, an annual tribute student. His mother was née Yang. His mother alone was living. His elder brother was Han, and his younger brothers were Cheng and Zhu. He married a woman née Cheng. He placed one hundred thirty-third in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and three hundred sixth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Shen Yuncheng 沈允成, courtesy name Ruxian, was registered in a civilian household in Deqing County, Huzhou Prefecture, Zhejiang. A supplementary student of the county Confucian school specializing in the Book of Documents, he was fifth in birth order, aged thirty-four, and born on the eleventh day of the sixth month. His great-grandfather was Zhen; his grandfather, Ren; and his father, Qi, a Professor in a Confucian school. His mother was née Ma. His father alone was living. His elder brothers were Song, a Right Assistant Administration Commissioner; Geng; Shi; and Tan. He married a woman née Ni. He placed fifty-sixth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and two hundred twenty-first in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Hong Shengyuan, registered in a military household of Heyang Guard [?], Shuntian Prefecture, was originally from Huangyan County, Zhejiang. An additional student at the prefectural school, he specialized in the Book of Documents; his courtesy name was Zishi, he ranked first among his brothers, and he was thirty-two years old, born on the eighth day of the ninth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Qing, his grandfather Ying, and his father Lun; his mother was née Gu and his stepmother née Xing. His parents and at least one grandparent were living. His younger brothers were Zhenyuan, Yuyuan, and Guangyuan. He married a woman née Yu and subsequently a woman née Qiao. He placed seventy-sixth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 205th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Liu Zhongli was registered in a civilian household of Yucheng County, Jinan Prefecture, Shandong. A student at the county school, he specialized in the Book of Documents; his courtesy name was Jianfu, he ranked first among his brothers, and he was thirty years old, born on the twenty-first day of the eighth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Hai, his grandfather Jun (an honorary official for public benefaction), and his father Gui; his mother was née Wang. His parents and at least one grandparent were living. He married a woman née Wei. He placed fifty-third in the Shandong Provincial Examination and 372nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Chen Yidian, registered in an official household of Tengchong Guard, Yongchang Prefecture, Yunnan, was originally from Deyang County, Sichuan. A student at the Tengyue Department school, he specialized in the Book of Rites; his courtesy name was Yuandun, he ranked first among his brothers, and he was twenty-five years old, born on the seventeenth day of the sixth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Jing, his grandfather Hao (an honorary official recognized for longevity), and his father Mingli (an Assistant Instructor); his mother was née Yin. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Yixun, Yixian, and Yiding. He placed fourteenth in the Yunnan Provincial Examination and 362nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Liu Zhu, registered in a civilian household of Gong'an County, Jingzhou Prefecture, Huguang, was originally from Nanchang County, Jiangxi. A student at the Gong'an County school, he specialized in the Book of Odes; his courtesy name was Haiweng, he ranked fourth among his brothers, and he was fifty-seven years old, born on the twenty-seventh day of the tenth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Zan, his grandfather Chongzheng, and his father Qingshan; his mother was née Wang. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Bao, Bi, and Yu, and his younger brothers were Xi, Gong, and Fan. He married a woman née Guo. He placed sixteenth in the Huguang Provincial Examination and eighty-first in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Shi Yingyue, registered in an official household in Longyan County, Zhangzhou Prefecture, Fujian, was a native of Lai’an County, Zhili. A student of the Directorate of Education, he specialized in the Book of Changes. His courtesy name was Zhongxian; he ranked first in the family and was thirty-one years old, born on the nineteenth day of the ninth month. His great-grandfather Kun, grandfather Zheng, and father Zhen were all company commanders; his mother was née Lin. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Yingsong, Yingqi, and Yingqiao, and his wife was née Qiu. He placed 107th in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 286th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Xia Qian was registered in a commoner household in Changyuan County, Daming Prefecture, Zhili. A student of the Directorate of Education, he specialized in the Book of Changes. His courtesy name was Kongzhao; he ranked first in the family and was thirty-one years old, born on the eleventh day of the ninth month. His great-grandfather was You, his grandfather Chen, and his father Feng; his mother was née Song. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Gang and Jiang, his younger brother was Tuan, and his wife was née Wang. He placed 115th in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 304th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Ren Shi was registered in a military household in Zhouzhi County, Xi’an Prefecture, Shaanxi. A county school student, he specialized in the Spring and Autumn Annals. His courtesy name was Xueyou; he ranked first in the family and was thirty-six years old, born on the third day of the fifth month. His great-grandfather was Fang, his grandfather Qi, and his father Zizhi, a subprefectural clerk; his mother was née Jiao. His mother alone survived. His younger brothers were Hua and Ru, and his wife was née Zhao. He placed thirty-sixth in the Shaanxi Provincial Examination and 225th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Lu Yilin was registered in a commoner household in Ba County, Chongqing Prefecture, Sichuan. A county school student, he specialized in the Book of Documents. His courtesy name was Zhenfu; he ranked first in the family and was thirty-one years old, born on the eighteenth day of the first month. His great-grandfather was Zhongqi, his grandfather Xiang, and his father Yanghao; his mother was née Zhou. His grandparents and parents were living. His younger brothers were Yilong, Yizhi, Yiguan, and Yicheng. His wife was née Zhang, and he subsequently married a woman née Wang. He placed forty-sixth in the Sichuan Provincial Examination and 160th in the Metropolitan Examination.

He was an added student of the county Confucian school and specialized in the Book of Documents. His courtesy name was Chongwen, and he was the eldest among his brothers. He was thirty-four years old, born on the twenty-eighth day of the sixth month. His great-grandfather was Jian; his grandfather was Xiang, who held an honorary title for longevity; his father was Bangning; and his mother was née Wang. His grandparents and parents were all living. His younger brothers were Congming, Congjun, Congxia, and Congshi. His wife was née Liu. He placed twenty-fifth in the Shaanxi Provincial Examination and 366th in the Metropolitan Examination.

title: 隆慶五年進士登科錄
text:
皇帝制曰朕昭承
天命纘御丕基五年
於兹夙夜皇皇圖
惟治理每思與天
下共享和平之福
===
===
而未臻厥效朕甚
惑之黃虞尚矣三
代以成周為盛說
者謂太和在其宇
宙果何道以致之
alt_text:
皇帝制曰朕昭承
天命纘御丕基五年
於玆夙夜皇皇圖
惟治理每思與天
下共亨和平之福
===
而未臻厥效朕甚
惑之黃虞尚矣三
代以成周爲盛說
者謂太和在其宇
宙果何道以致之
punctuated: 皇帝制曰：朕昭承天命，纘御丕基，五年於兹。夙夜皇皇，圖惟治理，每思與天下共享和平之福，而未臻厥效，朕甚惑之。黃虞尚矣，三代以成周為盛。說者謂太和在其宇宙，果何道以致之？
translation_en: The Emperor's decree reads: I have reverently received Heaven’s mandate and succeeded to the throne of this great imperial foundation, now for five years. Anxiously attentive morning and night, I deliberate upon good government, ever wishing to share the blessings of peace and harmony with all under Heaven. Yet these results have not been attained, and I am deeply perplexed by this. The ages of Huangdi and Shun are remote indeed; among the Three Dynasties, the fully established Zhou was the most flourishing. Commentators say that supreme harmony prevailed throughout its realm. By what way, truly, was this achieved?

title: 隆慶五年進士登科錄
text:
或謂周禮九職八
則五禮六樂三物
六容使民勤事而
不暇習於上下等
威之中消其尊崇
===
富侈之心是以化
行俗美天下和平
然歟否歟漢治號
為近古當其時獻
議之臣猶有欲定

富侈之心是以化
行俗美天下和平
然歟否歟漢治號
為近古當其時獻
議之臣猶有欲定
punctuated: 或謂《周禮》九職、八則、五禮、六樂、三物、六容，使民勤事而不暇，習於上下等威之中，消其尊崇富侈之心，是以化行俗美，天下和平。然歟？否歟？漢治號為近古，當其時，獻議之臣猶有欲定
translation_en: Some say that the nine occupations, eight regulations, five rites, six musical traditions, three subjects of instruction, and six modes of deportment in the Rites of Zhou (Zhou li) kept the people diligently occupied with their duties, leaving them no idle time, and accustomed them to the graded distinctions of rank and dignity between superior and inferior. These dispelled their desire for exalted status, wealth, and extravagance. Thus moral transformation spread, customs became good, and peace and harmony prevailed throughout the realm. Was this so, or was it not? Government under the Han is reputed to have approached that of antiquity. Yet even then, among the ministers who submitted proposals, there were those who wished to establish…

title: 隆慶五年進士登科錄
text:
經制者欲建萬世
之業者欲不嚴而
成化者之三臣者
皆病徒法不足以
興治然則如何而
===
可以致太平歟洪
惟我
太祖高皇帝開天建
極六合同風以政
防民若職掌所載
alt_text:
經制者欲建萬世
之業者欲不嚴而
成化者之三臣者
皆病徒法不足以
興治然則如何而
===
可以致太平歟洪
惟我
太祖高皇帝開天建
極六合同風以政
防民若職掌所載
punctuated:
經制者，欲建萬世之業者，欲不嚴而成化者，之三臣者，皆病徒法不足以興治。然則如何而可以致太平歟？
洪惟我太祖高皇帝，開天建極，六合同風，以政防民，若《職掌》所載。
translation_en:
…establish enduring institutions, those who wished to build an undertaking lasting ten thousand generations, and those who wished to transform the people without severity: these three ministers [?] all considered laws alone insufficient to bring about good government. How, then, could Great Peace be achieved?
We reverently reflect that our Emperor Taizu Gao inaugurated a new age and established the supreme standard, bringing uniform customs throughout the realm. He used administrative measures to restrain the people, as recorded in Official Responsibilities (Zhizhang)…

title: 隆慶五年進士登科錄
text:
同符六典以禮教
民若
洪武禮制禮儀定式
大明集禮所載制
度精詳達於上下
===
可萬世行之而寡
過矣乃今治績罔
效風教未孚長厚
之意薄虛偽之習
滋民或侈泰以相
alt_text:
同符六典以禮教
民若
洪武禮制禮儀定式
大明集禮所載制
度精詳達於上下
===
可萬世行之而寡
過矣乃令治績罔
效風教未孚長厚
之意薄虛偽之習
滋民或侈泰以相
punctuated: 同符六典；以禮教民，若《洪武禮制》《禮儀定式》《大明集禮》所載，制度精詳，達於上下，可萬世行之而寡過矣。乃今治績罔效，風教未孚，長厚之意薄，虛偽之習滋，民或侈泰以相
translation_en: …in accord with the Six Canons; he instructed the people through ritual, as recorded in the Ritual Institutions of the Hongwu Reign, the Prescribed Forms of Ritual and Ceremony, and the Collected Rites of the Great Ming. These institutions were precise and comprehensive, extending to those above and below; they could be practiced for ten thousand generations with few failings. Yet now governance yields no results, moral instruction has not won the people's trust, the spirit of generosity and kindness has weakened, and habits of falsehood and hypocrisy have increased. Some among the people indulge in extravagance to vie with one another…

title: 隆慶五年進士登科錄
text:
炫士或睢恣以陵
上庶幾所謂卿大
夫和於朝士庶人
和於野者而不可
得豈政之文徒具
===
而禮之實未至歟
今欲興敎化厚風
俗使天下志慮不
易視聽純一相安
於蕩蕩平平之治

和於野者而不可
得豈政之文徒具
===
而禮之實未至歟
令欲興教化厚風
俗使天下志慮不
易視聽純一相安
於蕩蕩平平之治
punctuated: 炫，士或睢恣以陵上。庶幾所謂「卿大夫和於朝，士庶人和於野」者，而不可得。豈政之文徒具，而禮之實未至歟？今欲興敎化，厚風俗，使天下志慮不易，視聽純一，相安於蕩蕩平平之治，
translation_en: …outshine one another in ostentation, while some scholars act insolently and defy their superiors. We hope to attain what is called “harmony among ministers and great officers at court, and harmony among scholars and commoners outside the court,” yet cannot achieve it. Could it be that the outward forms of government are merely in place, while the substance of ritual propriety has yet to be realized? Now we wish to promote moral instruction and enrich customary morality, so that throughout the realm people remain steadfast in their purposes and thoughts, are pure and unified in what they see and hear, and live together in contentment under broad and impartial governance…

title: 隆慶五年進士登科錄
text:
臣張元忭
臣對臣聞帝王之繼天而立極也有齊一天
下之具而後可以臻治平之效有化成天下
之實而後可以追協和之風政也者齊一天
下之具也所以示民之趨而嚴其防者也禮
也者化成天下之實也所以定民之志而彰
其教者也政之所布或止於法制之粗而禮
之所陳不足以建中和之極則民皆習於其
文而昧乎其實雖欲使之志慮不易視聽純
一以相安於蕩蕩平平之化胡可得哉是故
===
聖哲之君受上天之寄膺化民之責不徒道
之以制度文為之具而必有禮焉以寓夫潛
孚默運之機勸民之善而不以爵祿遏民之
惡而不以刑威是以其教不言而喻其民不
令而行布列於庶官者各修其職而不曰志
于尊榮散處於族黨者各安其分而不曰志
于富侈遵王道者無偏黨頗僻之患若聖訓
者有時雍風動之休古之帝王所以垂拱而
治揖讓而化者其有由然哉欽惟
皇帝陛下

臣對：臣聞帝王之繼天而立極也，有齊一天下之具，而後可以臻治平之效；有化成天下之實，而後可以追協和之風。政也者，齊一天下之具也，所以示民之趨而嚴其防者也；禮也者，化成天下之實也，所以定民之志而彰其教者也。政之所布，或止於法制之粗，而禮之所陳，不足以建中和之極，則民皆習於其文而昧乎其實。雖欲使之志慮不易，視聽純一，以相安於蕩蕩平平之化，胡可得哉？是故聖哲之君，受上天之寄，膺化民之責，不徒道之以制度文為之具，而必有禮焉，以寓夫潛孚默運之機。勸民之善而不以爵祿，遏民之惡而不以刑威，是以其教不言而喻，其民不令而行。布列於庶官者，各修其職，而不曰志于尊榮；散處於族黨者，各安其分，而不曰志于富侈。遵王道者，無偏黨頗僻之患；若聖訓者，有時雍風動之休。古之帝王所以垂拱而治、揖讓而化者，其有由然哉！欽惟皇帝陛下……
translation_en:
Your servant Zhang Yuanbian.

Your servant replies: I have heard that emperors and kings, in succeeding Heaven and establishing the supreme standard, must possess the means to bring all under Heaven into unity before they can achieve orderly and peaceful government; they must possess the substance that transforms and perfects all under Heaven before they can emulate the spirit of concord and harmony. Government is the means of bringing all under Heaven into unity: it shows the people the course they should pursue and makes strict the restraints upon them. Ritual is the substance that transforms and perfects all under Heaven: it steadies the people's resolve and makes manifest the teachings intended for them. If the measures of government extend only to the outward framework of laws and institutions, and the rites set forth are insufficient to establish the supreme standard of equilibrium and harmony, then the people will all become accustomed to outward forms while remaining ignorant of their substance. Even if one wished to make their intentions and thoughts unwavering, their seeing and hearing pure and single-minded, so that they might dwell together in contentment under a transformation broad and impartial, how could this be achieved?

Thus a sage and enlightened ruler, receiving the trust of Heaven above and bearing responsibility for transforming the people, does not guide them merely through institutions and formal observances. He must also employ ritual, embodying within it the workings of influence that wins trust unseen and operates silently. He encourages goodness among the people without using ranks and stipends, and restrains their wrongdoing without using the terrors of punishment. Consequently, his teaching is understood without words, and his people act without commands. Those appointed to the various offices each attend to their duties, without declaring an ambition for exalted standing and glory; those dwelling among clans and local communities each rest content with their allotted station, without declaring an ambition for wealth and extravagance. Those who follow the kingly Way are free of the evils of partiality, faction, bias, and perversity; those who obey the sages' instructions enjoy the blessings of prevailing harmony and a transforming influence that moves like the wind. Surely there was a reason why the emperors and kings of antiquity could govern with their robes hanging loosely and their hands folded, and transform the people through deference and yielding! I reverently consider that Your Majesty the Emperor…

title: 隆慶五年進士登科錄
text:
聰明天啟
仁儉性成紀綱振舉于
朝廷而海宇嚮風
威德覃敷於邊塞而蠻夷率俾治已至矣化已
洽矣乃於
萬幾之暇進臣等而策之慨然有慕于成周之
治而以方今之民風士習為憂詢臣等以興
禮化民之要誠求治無已望道未見之盛心
也草茅之士沐浴
聖化願攄忠悃之日久矣敢不披瀝以對書曰天
===
降下民作之君作之師惟曰其助上帝寵之
四方又曰惟皇上帝降衷于下民若有恒性
克綏厥猷惟后盖四海之廣萬民之衆風土
異宜習俗異尚不有以整齊之則亂不有以
約束之則爭君人者荷帝天之命握君師之
權以立極於萬民者也則凡所以懸之象魏
頒之條教彰之物采陳之藝極以整齊天下
約束天下而使之順軌嚮方焉者寧非治天
下之常經也哉然此特治天下之文而興禮
敦讓則化天下之實也有其文而孚之以實

punctuated:
聰明天啟，仁儉性成。紀綱振舉于朝廷，而海宇嚮風；威德覃敷於邊塞，而蠻夷率俾。治已至矣，化已洽矣。乃於萬幾之暇，進臣等而策之，慨然有慕于成周之治，而以方今之民風士習為憂，詢臣等以興禮化民之要，誠求治無已、望道未見之盛心也。草茅之士，沐浴聖化，願攄忠悃之日久矣，敢不披瀝以對？
書曰：「天降下民，作之君，作之師，惟曰其助上帝寵之四方。」又曰：「惟皇上帝，降衷于下民，若有恒性，克綏厥猷惟后。」盖四海之廣，萬民之衆，風土異宜，習俗異尚，不有以整齊之則亂，不有以約束之則爭。君人者，荷帝天之命，握君師之權，以立極於萬民者也。則凡所以懸之象魏，頒之條教，彰之物采，陳之藝極，以整齊天下、約束天下，而使之順軌嚮方焉者，寧非治天下之常經也哉？然此特治天下之文，而興禮敦讓，則化天下之實也。有其文而孚之以實，
translation_en:
…Heaven has endowed you with intelligence, and benevolence and frugality are inherent in your nature. The guiding principles of government have been reinvigorated at court, and all within the seas turn toward your influence. Your might and virtue extend throughout the frontier regions, and the non-Chinese peoples all submit [?]. Order has already reached its height, and your transforming influence has already spread everywhere. Yet, in an interval amid your myriad affairs, you have summoned us, your servants, and posed a policy question. Earnestly admiring the governance of the Zhou at its flourishing height, and concerned about the present customs of the people and habits of scholars, you have asked us about the essentials of promoting ritual propriety and transforming the people. This truly manifests your noble resolve to seek good government without cease and to pursue the Way as though you had yet to perceive it. We scholars from humble obscurity, having basked in your sage transforming influence, have long wished for the day when we might express our loyal sincerity. How could we dare not lay bare our hearts in reply?
The Book of Documents says: “Heaven brought forth the common people and established rulers and teachers for them, intending that these should assist the Lord on High in cherishing them throughout the four quarters.” It also says: “The august Lord on High bestowed an inner moral norm upon the common people. In accordance with their constant nature, it is the sovereign alone who can bring them securely along their proper path.” Across the vastness of the four seas and among the multitude of people, local conditions call for different practices, and customs favor different things. Without means to bring them into order, there will be disorder; without means to restrain them, there will be contention. The ruler of men bears the mandate of Heaven, holds the authority of both ruler and teacher, and establishes the supreme standard for all the people. Thus, displaying ordinances upon the palace gate towers, promulgating regulations and instructions, making distinctions manifest through ceremonial objects and colors, and setting forth standards of accomplishment—all means of ordering and restraining the realm so that its people follow the proper course and turn toward the right direction—are these not the constant principles for governing the realm? Yet these are only the outward forms of governing the realm; promoting ritual propriety and fostering deference are the substance of transforming it. If one possesses these outward forms and makes them effective through substance…

于仁讓之治不務其實而徒飾之以文則革
其面者未必能一其志而天下卒積習于偷
靡之風上之所尚少異下之所趨頓殊故曰
政刑者輔治之具德禮者致治之本而治天
下者貴審所尚也黃虞之治邈哉弗可復覩
矣試以成周言之周自文武開之於前周公
成之於後其所以治天下之具斟酌百王損
益二代綱之紀之經之綸之盖纖悉備矣乃
其化民之實則有不盡於是者是故樸棫作
===

播其忠厚儉勤之化者真懇惻怛盖不徒政
以驅之而恒有禮以率之也嘗觀周禮一書
周公以之相七年之治成王以之享四十年
之太平有周以之培八百年之命脉斯誠治
天下之大綱大要也然不徒曰周之政典而
以禮名之則其寓意遠矣今考其所載若設
官分職辨方正位體國經野制度品式非不
詳且密也而其精蘊所存機要所急則惓惓
乎以禮化民之是務焉是故任之以九職治

…then the measures that regulate people’s outward conduct also reach their hearts, and all under Heaven are gradually cultivated into a state of benevolence and deference. If one neglects this substance and merely embellishes outward forms, measures that change people’s outward demeanor may not unite their intentions, and all under Heaven will ultimately become habituated to laxity and extravagance. A slight difference in what those above esteem brings a marked divergence in what those below pursue. Thus it is said: administration and punishments are instruments that assist government; virtue and ritual are the foundations of good government. Those who govern all under Heaven must therefore carefully consider what they esteem.
The government of Huangdi and Shun is so remote that it can no longer be witnessed! Let us instead consider the perfected Zhou order. Kings Wen and Wu initiated it, and the Duke of Zhou subsequently brought it to completion. In devising its instruments for governing all under Heaven, they weighed the practices of the many earlier kings and adapted those of the two preceding dynasties, organizing and arranging everything until even the smallest details were provided for. Yet the substance of their moral transformation of the people was not exhausted by these measures. Thus, the teaching that nurtured worthy men in “The Oak Trees” (Pu yu), the intent of “The Ospreys’ Cry” (Guan ju) and “The Qilin’s Hooves” (Lin zhi), and the virtue of “The Reeds” (Xing wei) and “The Tall Southernwood” (Liao xiao) spread the transforming influence of loyalty, generosity, frugality, and diligence with genuine sincerity and heartfelt concern. They did not merely drive the people by administrative measures, but constantly led them through ritual.
I have examined the book Rites of Zhou. Through it, the Duke of Zhou assisted in seven years of government; through it, King Cheng enjoyed forty years of peace; and through it, the Zhou dynasty nourished the lifeblood of its eight-hundred-year mandate. This is indeed the great framework and essential foundation for governing all under Heaven. Yet it is not simply called the administrative code of Zhou: its title invokes ritual, and the significance embodied in this is profound. Examining its contents, we find that its establishment of offices and division of duties, determination of directions and proper positions, layout of the capital and demarcation of the countryside, and institutional rules and standards are both detailed and exact. Yet its innermost meaning and most urgent priorities lie in its devoted pursuit of transforming the people through ritual. Thus it assigns them the nine occupations and governs…

三物正之以六容以功詔祿而尊卑之有等

長習于升降揖讓之節而囿于道德仁義之
中曉然知上下之分如冠履之不可踰位巖
廊之上者懷素餐之懼效靖共之忠而卿大
夫相與和于朝處邦國之中者泯僭侈之私

美比屋可封宋儒謂太和在成周宇宙間詎
非以禮化民之明效也哉易曰上天下澤履
===

君也知乎此則成周之所以化行俗美天下
和平者其道可知而後之圖治者可以知所

然復古之治而本之躬行以善其則先之禮
教以孚其心則成周太和之治幾可再見奈
何以雜伯之心而行一切苟且之政黃老申
韓既以陰壞天下之學術而恭顯許史又以
紊亂先王之典刑是以當時獻議之臣若賈

和平者其道可知而後之圖治者可以知所
務矣漢之興也去周未遠使當時之君能奮
然復古之治而本之躬行以善其則先之禮
教以孚其心則成周太和之治幾可再見奈
何以雜伯之心而行一切苟且之政黃老申
韓既以陰壞天下之學術而恭顯許史又以
紊亂先王之典刑是以當時獻議之臣若賈
punctuated:
之以八則，節之以五禮，和之以六樂，迪之以三物，正之以六容，以功詔祿，而尊卑之有等；以事奠食，而貴賤之有章。當時之民，自少至長，習于升降揖讓之節，而囿于道德仁義之中，曉然知上下之分，如冠履之不可踰。位巖廊之上者，懷素餐之懼，效靖共之忠，而卿大夫相與和于朝；處邦國之中者，泯僭侈之私，敦雍睦之義，而士庶人相與和于野。風俗之美，比屋可封。宋儒謂太和在成周宇宙間，詎非以禮化民之明效也哉？《易》曰：「上天下澤，履。君子以辨上下，定民志。」《記》曰：「君臣上下父子兄弟，非禮不定。」「禮者，君之大柄，所以治政安君也。」知乎此，則成周之所以化行俗美、天下和平者，其道可知，而後之圖治者可以知所務矣。
漢之興也，去周未遠。使當時之君能奮然復古之治，而本之躬行以善其則，先之禮教以孚其心，則成周太和之治幾可再見。奈何以雜伯之心而行一切苟且之政，黃老申韓既以陰壞天下之學術，而恭顯許史又以紊亂先王之典刑。是以當時獻議之臣，若賈

…govern them through the eight regulations, regulate them through the five rites, harmonize them through the six musical traditions, guide them through the three subjects of instruction, and correct their bearing through the six forms of deportment. Emoluments were assigned according to merit, so that higher and lower ranks had their gradations; provisions were determined according to duties, so that noble and humble stations had their distinctions. The people of that time, from youth to maturity, practiced the prescribed forms of ascending and descending, bowing and yielding precedence, and lived within the bounds of the Way, virtue, benevolence, and righteousness. They clearly understood the distinctions between superior and inferior, as inviolable as the respective places of cap and shoes. Those occupying positions at court feared drawing sustenance without rendering service and devoted themselves loyally and reverently to their duties; thus ministers and grand officers lived in harmony at court. Those dwelling throughout the states suppressed selfish impulses toward usurpation and extravagance and cultivated concord and mutual affection; thus gentlemen and commoners lived in harmony in the countryside. Customs were so admirable that every household was worthy of receiving a fief. Song Confucian scholars said that supreme harmony pervaded the universe in the perfected Zhou order. Was this not clear evidence of the efficacy of transforming the people through ritual?
The Book of Changes says: “Heaven above, the marsh below: Treading. The gentleman thereby distinguishes superior from inferior and settles the people’s aspirations.” The Record of Rites says: “Ruler and minister, superior and inferior, father and son, elder and younger brother: without ritual, their relationships cannot be established.” It also says: “Ritual is the ruler’s great instrument, by which government is ordered and the ruler secured.” Once this is understood, one can understand the way by which the perfected Zhou order spread moral transformation, refined customs, and brought peace and harmony to all under Heaven. Those in later ages who seek good government can then know where to direct their efforts.
When the Han arose, it was not far removed from the Zhou. Had the rulers of that time resolutely restored the government of antiquity, grounding it in their own conduct to provide a worthy example and leading with ritual instruction to win the people’s trust, the supremely harmonious government of the perfected Zhou order might almost have been seen again. Yet why did they, with minds tainted by hegemonic ambition, pursue nothing but expedient and makeshift policies? The teachings of Huang-Lao and of Shen Buhai and Han Fei had already covertly corrupted learning throughout the realm, while Gong and Xian, and the Xu and Shi families, further disrupted the established standards of the former kings. title: 隆慶五年進士登科錄
text:
誼之於文帝則曰禮者禁于將然法者禁于
已然而欲其定經制厚風俗以興殷周之治
王吉之於宣帝則曰安上治民莫善于禮而
欲其述舊禮明王制以建萬世之策匡衡之
於元帝則曰道德之行自近者始而欲其陳
德義循禮讓不嚴而化以挽浮靡之趨蓋誠
以太平之效不可以徒法致而轉移化導之
微權必以禮教為之本也三臣之言豈非通
達治體者哉而漢之三君卒狃于陋習而不
能用是以德色誶語民鮮淳良之俗貪鄙嗜
===
利士無廉靖之風居官而致富者為雄傑處
奸而得利者為壯士有如賈誼之所太息貢
禹之所極論者終漢之世日以陵夷而不振
非漢之民不若成周也禮教不修而文法之
弊滋也洪惟我
太祖高皇帝肇造區夏驅逐胡元復帝王所自立
之土宇建古今所未有之事功不惟政以防
民而又禮以教民蓋有兼舉而不遺者以政
言之若諸司職掌所載官以職分而九卿百
執事之相維事以類繁而大小纖悉之畢舉

執事之相維事以類繫而大小纖悉之畢舉
punctuated:
誼之於文帝，則曰：「禮者禁于將然，法者禁于已然。」而欲其定經制、厚風俗，以興殷周之治。王吉之於宣帝，則曰：「安上治民，莫善于禮。」而欲其述舊禮、明王制，以建萬世之策。匡衡之於元帝，則曰：「道德之行，自近者始。」而欲其陳德義、循禮讓，不嚴而化，以挽浮靡之趨。蓋誠以太平之效不可以徒法致，而轉移化導之微權，必以禮教為之本也。三臣之言，豈非通達治體者哉？而漢之三君卒狃于陋習而不能用，是以德色誶語，民鮮淳良之俗；貪鄙嗜利，士無廉靖之風。居官而致富者為雄傑，處奸而得利者為壯士。有如賈誼之所太息、貢禹之所極論者，終漢之世，日以陵夷而不振。非漢之民不若成周也，禮教不修，而文法之弊滋也。
洪惟我太祖高皇帝肇造區夏，驅逐胡元，復帝王所自立之土宇，建古今所未有之事功。不惟政以防民，而又禮以教民，蓋有兼舉而不遺者。以政言之，若《諸司職掌》所載，官以職分，而九卿百執事之相維；事以類繁，而大小纖悉之畢舉。
translation_en:
…Yi, addressing Emperor Wen, said: “Ritual prohibits wrongdoing before it occurs; law prohibits it after it has occurred.” He wished the emperor to establish enduring institutions and enrich social customs, thereby bringing about the good government of the Yin and Zhou. Wang Ji, addressing Emperor Xuan, said: “For securing the ruler’s position and governing the people, nothing surpasses ritual.” He wished the emperor to follow the ancient rites and elucidate the institutions of the kings, thereby establishing a plan for ten thousand generations. Kuang Heng, addressing Emperor Yuan, said: “The practice of the Way and virtue begins with those closest at hand.” He wished the emperor to set forth virtue and righteousness and follow ritual and deference, transforming the people without severity and reversing the tendency toward frivolity and extravagance. They truly understood that the results of great peace could not be achieved through laws alone, and that the subtle means of transforming and guiding the people must be founded upon ritual instruction. Were not the words of these three ministers those of men thoroughly conversant with the essentials of government? Yet the three Han rulers remained habituated to inferior practices and could not put this counsel into effect. Consequently, self-satisfied looks and abusive speech prevailed, and the people seldom displayed pure and good customs; greed, baseness, and the appetite for profit prevailed, and the educated possessed no ethos of integrity and restraint. Those who became rich in office were considered outstanding men; those who profited through wrongdoing were considered men of prowess. Conditions such as those over which Jia Yi sighed deeply and which Gong Yu criticized at length continued throughout the Han, declining daily without recovery. It was not that the people of the Han were inferior to those of the Zhou at its height: ritual instruction was neglected, while the abuses of legal formalism multiplied.
We reverently reflect that our Emperor Taizu Gao founded his rule over the Chinese realm, expelled the foreign Yuan, restored the territory in which emperors and kings had established themselves, and accomplished deeds without precedent in ancient or modern times. He not only used government to restrain the people but also used ritual to instruct them, employing both and neglecting neither. As regards government, consider what is recorded in the Duties of the Various Offices (Zhusi zhizhang): offices were divided according to their responsibilities, with the Nine Ministers and all functionaries supporting one another; affairs were manifold in their categories [?], and matters great and small were all attended to, down to the finest detail…

title: 隆慶五年進士登科錄
text:
宏謨曲算燦然六典之章程也以禮言之若
洪武禮制禮儀定式大明集禮所載提其綱領
而祭享昏喪之有節析其條目而服舍器用
之有差良法美意藹然周官之矩範也二百
年來道化淪洽日氐月窟之邦含齒戴髮之
屬孰不沾德澤歌太平雖成周之盛何以加
此而
聖問所及猶以治績罔效風教未孚為慮臣嘗思
之而得其故矣蓋成周之所以化民成俗者
政非出于禮之外也我
===
聖祖之所以建極垂範者禮即寓於政之中也有
政以為齊一天下之具故有以一民之視聽
而孰非所以為禮之迹有禮以為化成天下
之實故有以定民之心志而孰非所以為政
之精然則昔之所以和平而今之所以偷靡
者從可知已由今之時觀之長厚者變而為
浮夸淳龐者變而為虛偽倡優忘后飾之僭
墻屋競文繡之觀而民之侈泰以相炫者日
甚也急進取則懷入市攫金之心工擠排則
為下穽投石之計而士之恣睢以陵上者可

宏謨曲算，燦然六典之章程也。以禮言之，若《洪武禮制》《禮儀定式》《大明集禮》所載，提其綱領，而祭享昏喪之有節；析其條目，而服舍器用之有差。良法美意，藹然《周官》之矩範也。二百年來，道化淪洽，日氐月窟之邦，含齒戴髮之屬，孰不沾德澤、歌太平？雖成周之盛，何以加此？而聖問所及，猶以治績罔效、風教未孚為慮。臣嘗思之，而得其故矣。蓋成周之所以化民成俗者，政非出于禮之外也。我聖祖之所以建極垂範者，禮即寓於政之中也。有政以為齊一天下之具，故有以一民之視聽，而孰非所以為禮之迹？有禮以為化成天下之實，故有以定民之心志，而孰非所以為政之精？然則昔之所以和平，而今之所以偷靡者，從可知已。

由今之時觀之，長厚者變而為浮夸，淳龐者變而為虛偽；倡優忘后飾之僭，墻屋競文繡之觀，而民之侈泰以相炫者日甚也。急進取，則懷入市攫金之心；工擠排，則為下穽投石之計，而士之恣睢以陵上者可
translation_en:
… Grand plans and meticulous calculations: these are the resplendent regulations of the Six Statutes. As for ritual, consider what is recorded in the Ritual System of the Hongwu Reign, the Established Forms of Ritual and Ceremony, and the Collected Rites of the Great Ming. Their overarching principles establish due measures for sacrifices, offerings, marriages, and funerals; their detailed provisions establish distinctions in clothing, dwellings, implements, and utensils. Their excellent laws and benevolent intentions fully embody the standards of the Offices of Zhou. For two hundred years, moral transformation has permeated everywhere. Among the countries at the sun’s extremity [?] and the moon’s cavern, among all creatures with teeth and hair, who has not received the blessings of imperial virtue and sung of Great Peace? Even the flourishing age of Zhou could scarcely surpass this. Yet Your Majesty’s question still expresses concern that government has produced no effective results and moral instruction has not won the people’s trust. Your servant has reflected upon this and discovered the reason. The Zhou transformed the people and established good customs because their government did not stand apart from ritual. Our sagely founding ancestor established the supreme standard and handed down exemplary models because ritual was embodied within government itself. Government provides the means to bring unity and order to all under Heaven, thereby unifying what the people see and hear: which of its workings is not a visible manifestation of ritual? Ritual provides the substance through which all under Heaven are transformed, thereby settling the people’s hearts and purposes: which of its workings is not the essence of government? Thus we can understand why there was harmony and peace in former times, but laxity and extravagance today.

Looking at the present, those once generous and sincere have become frivolous and boastful; those once simple and substantial have become false and deceitful. Entertainers and actors disregard the usurpation of rank involved in wearing a queen’s adornments [?]; walls and houses vie in displays of patterned and embroidered splendor. The people grow daily more extravagant in their efforts to dazzle one another. Eager for advancement, men harbor the impulse of one who enters the marketplace and snatches gold; skilled in pushing others aside, they devise schemes to cast stones upon someone fallen into a pit. And the unrestrained arrogance with which scholars defy their superiors can …

title: 隆慶五年進士登科錄
text:
駁也民風之薄惡士習之澆漓非惟廑
陛下之憂臣亦且憂之矣臣竊以為風俗之無良
者由教化之不明也教化之不明者由政本
之未立也夫所謂政之本者何也禮之實是
也今也詳法令而畧禮教重文藝而忽德行
賞罰非不明也而或枉其功過之實則下何
由而勸懲議論非不悉也而或歉于畫一之
守則下何由而趨避學校視為具員而師儒
之模範弗端守令勞于案牘而風俗之淳漓
罔念
===
陛下所謂政之文徒具而禮之實未至者臣不敢
謂無是也則又何恠乎民風士習之日趨於
弊而不古若哉夫
陛下知致弊之由則知所以救弊之道其道無他
亦曰務禮之實而已矣臣請申
聖祖之制法成周之規採漢臣之言興禮讓之教
掌銓衡者不徒以政績課殿最而必核其行
檢司登籲者不徒以詞章品高下而兼採其
德誼賞當賢罰當罪而勸懲昭明允之公執
體要崇本實而議論黜靡曼之弊董學校者

punctuated:
駁也。民風之薄惡，士習之澆漓，非惟廑陛下之憂，臣亦且憂之矣。臣竊以為，風俗之無良者，由教化之不明也；教化之不明者，由政本之未立也。夫所謂政之本者何也？禮之實是也。今也詳法令而畧禮教，重文藝而忽德行。賞罰非不明也，而或枉其功過之實，則下何由而勸懲？議論非不悉也，而或歉于畫一之守，則下何由而趨避？學校視為具員，而師儒之模範弗端；守令勞于案牘，而風俗之淳漓罔念。陛下所謂政之文徒具，而禮之實未至者，臣不敢謂無是也。則又何恠乎民風士習之日趨於弊，而不古若哉？

夫陛下知致弊之由，則知所以救弊之道。其道無他，亦曰務禮之實而已矣。臣請申聖祖之制，法成周之規，採漢臣之言，興禮讓之教。掌銓衡者，不徒以政績課殿最，而必核其行檢；司登籲者，不徒以詞章品高下，而兼採其德誼。賞當賢，罰當罪，而勸懲昭明允之公；執體要，崇本實，而議論黜靡曼之弊。董學校者，
translation_en:
… can be refuted [?]. The baseness of popular customs and the degeneration of scholars’ habits cause concern not only to Your Majesty; your servant, too, is troubled by them. Your servant humbly believes that customs are unsound because moral instruction has not been made clear, and moral instruction has not been made clear because the foundation of government has not been established. What is this foundation of government? It is the substance of ritual propriety. Today, laws and ordinances receive detailed attention, while instruction in ritual propriety is neglected; literary accomplishments are valued, while virtuous conduct is disregarded. Rewards and punishments are certainly clear, yet they sometimes misrepresent actual merits and faults: how, then, can those below be encouraged or deterred? Deliberations are certainly thorough, yet adherence to a consistent standard is sometimes lacking: how, then, can those below know what to pursue and what to avoid? Schools are regarded merely as posts to be filled, and their teachers fail to provide upright examples. Prefects and magistrates toil over paperwork without giving thought to whether customs are wholesome or corrupt. Your Majesty has spoken of the outward forms of government being fully present while the substance of ritual propriety remains unrealized; your servant dares not say that this condition does not exist. Why, then, should we wonder that popular customs and scholars’ habits grow worse by the day and fall short of antiquity?

Since Your Majesty knows what has caused these abuses, you also know the way to remedy them. That way is nothing other than attending to the substance of ritual propriety. Your servant asks that the institutions of the sagely founder be reaffirmed, the regulations of the Zhou in its flourishing age be taken as models, the counsel of Han ministers be adopted, and instruction in ritual propriety and deference be promoted. Those responsible for personnel selection should not merely rank officials’ performance from worst to best according to their administrative achievements; they must also scrutinize their conduct. Those responsible for promoting men to office [?] should not merely rank them by their literary compositions, but should also consider their virtue and rectitude. Let rewards accord with worthiness and punishments with offenses, so that encouragement and deterrence manifest the impartiality of enlightened and equitable judgment. Grasp the essentials and honor fundamentals and substance, so that deliberations eliminate the vice of ornate elaboration. Those who oversee the schools…

translation_en:
…must emulate Yang Cheng at the Directorate of Education and Hu Yuan in Huzhou, rather than merely fill their posts with petty, ineffectual mediocrity. Those administering prefectures and counties must emulate Qiu Xiang in transforming the people through virtue and Yanshou in shutting his doors to reflect upon his faults, rather than win a reputation for worthiness merely through paperwork and meeting administrative deadlines. Thus the highest ministers will strive to match Yang Wan’s simplicity, and meritorious nobles and imperial relatives will admire Ma Liao’s example. Thus high officials will uphold the integrity celebrated in “Lamb’s Wool,” and scholars and commoners will rest content in the moral influence of “The Cricket.” Above, men will assess one another by ritual propriety; below, they will live harmoniously with one another through it. Mutually emulating one another, dignified and orderly, joyful and untroubled, they will embody supreme harmony: its manifestation will belong not to the perfected Zhou alone, but to our own day. How fortunate your servant would be to witness such flourishing in person!

Nevertheless, achieving good government has a root, and establishing moral instruction has a source. It rests solely with Your Majesty to seek these in your own person and mind, thereby setting an example for officials and people. For the ruler’s person is the source of all moral transformation; throughout the realm and beyond, to the bounds of the seas, all turn toward him and take him as their model.

If, while enjoying an age of fulfilled prosperity, he should forget the dangers of ease and desire—whether through music and sensual pleasures, cherished curiosities, or excursions and hunts—if he should sink into comfortable leisure without recognizing it, and reject loyal and worthy men without trusting them, then the very source of moral transformation would already be obstructed. How could one then hope for customs to return to simplicity? Your servant wishes that Your Majesty would rectify the root and purify the source, clear your mind and restrain your desires, thereby nurturing the foundation for a long reign and long life; guard against complacency and esteem frugality, thereby furthering the means of ensuring sufficiency for the state and the people; draw close each day to worthy assistants and deliberate calmly with them, jointly planning the work of bringing about great peace; and draw near each day to Confucian officials, repeatedly examining and discussing matters with them, so as to ponder deeply the source of moral transformation and good government. text:
宮闈休聲訖乎遐邇則教化所敷如風行而草
偃表正而景端所以享和平之福追成周之
盛者端不外此臣愚不識忌諱干冒
宸嚴不勝戰兢隕越之至臣謹對

translation_en: …within the palace, and a reputation for virtue reaches far and near, then wherever moral instruction spreads, it will be as grass bending before the wind, or a shadow falling straight when its gnomon is upright. The means of enjoying the blessings of peace and harmony and matching the flourishing age of the Zhou lie entirely in this. Your servant, in his ignorance, does not understand what must not be said and has presumed to offend Your Majesty’s august dignity. I am overcome with trembling and fear of falling into disgrace. Your servant respectfully submits this reply.

title: 隆慶五年進士登科錄
text:
臣劉瑊
臣對臣聞帝王之御世也必明乎禮之文而
後可以植天下之防必崇乎禮之本而後可
以成天下之化何也禮原於天則具於人心
而制於聖人其顯設於文物者則為禮之文
焉文以立政秩然而不亂天下所以率履而
範圍之者此其準也其涵蓄於本體者則為
禮之本焉本以立教渾然而不漓天下所以
潜孚而默感之者此其機也彼徒見夫禮之
文可以軌物而無見於禮之本乃以端軌則
===
品式雖詳而倡導之機不至等威雖峻而鼓
舞之術弗神天下之循法奉令以遵其不可
犯之防者或有之而望其革心易慮以趨於
無所勉之化則難矣聖人知其然其所以防
民者固必明乎制度典章以一天下之趨而
其所以化民者尤必本之精神心術以洽天
下之志此其成禮讓之風躋太和之俗而懿
美蓁隆之治卓乎其無以尚也後世守文之
君願治之主誠欲以禮教天下者修其文而
必敦其本焉孰謂五三帝王之治不可復見

punctuated:
臣劉瑊。

臣對：臣聞帝王之御世也，必明乎禮之文，而後可以植天下之防；必崇乎禮之本，而後可以成天下之化。何也？禮原於天，則具於人心，而制於聖人。其顯設於文物者，則為禮之文焉。文以立政，秩然而不亂，天下所以率履而範圍之者，此其準也。其涵蓄於本體者，則為禮之本焉。本以立教，渾然而不漓，天下所以潜孚而默感之者，此其機也。彼徒見夫禮之文可以軌物，而無見於禮之本乃以端軌則，品式雖詳，而倡導之機不至；等威雖峻，而鼓舞之術弗神。天下之循法奉令，以遵其不可犯之防者，或有之；而望其革心易慮，以趨於無所勉之化，則難矣。聖人知其然，其所以防民者，固必明乎制度典章，以一天下之趨；而其所以化民者，尤必本之精神心術，以洽天下之志。此其成禮讓之風，躋太和之俗，而懿美蓁隆之治，卓乎其無以尚也。後世守文之君、願治之主，誠欲以禮教天下者，修其文而必敦其本焉。孰謂五三帝王之治不可復見
translation_en:
Your servant Liu Jian.

Your servant replies: I have heard that, in governing the world, emperors and kings must understand the outward forms of ritual before they can establish restraints throughout the realm; they must exalt the foundations of ritual before they can bring about the moral transformation of the realm. Why is this? Ritual originates in Heaven, its principles are inherent in the human heart, and its institutions are fashioned by sages. What is visibly expressed in ceremonial objects and forms constitutes ritual’s outward aspect. Through these forms, government is established, orderly and free from confusion: they provide the standard by which all under Heaven follow proper conduct and are kept within its bounds. What is contained within its essential substance constitutes ritual’s foundation. Through this foundation, moral instruction is established, whole and undiluted: it is the vital means by which all under Heaven are inwardly won over and silently moved.

Those who see only that ritual’s outward forms can regulate conduct, but fail to see that its foundation is what makes those rules correct, may have detailed gradations and prescriptions, yet lack the vital means of giving moral leadership; their distinctions of rank and authority may be strict, yet their methods of inspiring people lack spiritual efficacy. There may be people throughout the realm who follow the laws and obey commands, observing restraints that must not be transgressed. But to expect them to reform their hearts and change their thinking, advancing toward a moral transformation that requires no exertion, would be difficult.

The sages understood this. In restraining the people, they necessarily clarified institutions, regulations, and established statutes, so as to unite the direction of the realm. But in transforming the people, they above all grounded their work in the spirit and the workings of the heart, so as to bring the aspirations of all under Heaven into harmony. Thus they established a prevailing spirit of ritual propriety and deference, raised customary conduct to supreme harmony, and achieved a splendid and flourishing government so outstanding that nothing could surpass it. If later rulers who preserve inherited institutions and sovereigns who aspire to good government truly wish to instruct the realm through ritual, they must cultivate its outward forms while strengthening its foundations. Who would say that the government of the Five Emperors and Three Kings could not be seen again …

translation_en:
…in the present day? Reverently considering Your Majesty the Emperor: you gloriously preside over the august realm and have received Heaven’s precious mandate. You follow the exemplary course of the ancient emperors and kings and take as your guide the established laws of your ancestors. Diligent in studying the teachings and attending to government, you undertake these tasks personally through cold and heat alike; you tirelessly hear and accept loyal advice and excellent counsel. The highest ministers and all officials observe ritual below with cultured refinement, while the sage Son of Heaven exalts ritual above with dignified harmony. Within there is peace, and beyond the borders tranquility; the seasons are propitious and the harvests abundant. The barbarians [?] come to court, and victories are reported from the torrid wilderness. Truly, it may be said that great ritual accords with the measured order of Heaven and Earth, and that through your profound reverence all under Heaven is at peace. Yet you have still summoned us, your servants, to court and graciously bestowed upon us your discerning questions. Earnestly wishing to transform all under Heaven through ritual and to share with everyone the blessings of harmony and peace, you remain dissatisfied that these effects have not yet been attained. Such is Your Majesty’s exalted resolve: you seek the Way as though you had not yet glimpsed it, and pursue good government without cease.
Your servant, dwelling obscurely among the common people, has witnessed the abuses of the age. I too have been moved by the way ritual’s outward forms daily gain ascendancy while its foundations daily diminish, and have never failed to sigh over this even in your sagely age. How could I dare not lay bare my thoughts, to respond to and extol even one ten-thousandth of your gracious command? text:

讓為國乎何有不能以禮讓為國如禮何夫
以民志之定而由於制禮以辨上下則禮之
文乃所以植天下之防者也不可以不明也
然以國家之治而由於禮讓則禮之本尤所

子以辨上下，定民志。及讀《魯論》，則曰：「能以禮讓為國乎？何有？不能以禮讓為國，如禮何？」夫以民志之定而由於制禮以辨上下，則禮之文乃所以植天下之防者也，不可以不明也。然以國家之治而由於禮讓，則禮之本尤所以成天下之化者也，不可以不崇也。故昔唐虞之世，如《二典》所紀，律度量衡，授時齊政，修禮如器，其禮文固已著也。然必曰「允恭克讓」焉，必曰「温恭允塞」焉。夫制禮而原於恭，是禮之行於帝廷者，不惟其文，惟其本。故當其時，黎民於變而為協和之美，四方從欲而為風動之休。胡氏謂太和在唐虞宇宙間，盖唐虞之太和，致之以禮讓而已矣。
迨夫成周之隆，如《周禮》所載，九職八則，五禮六樂，三物六容，其禮文固尤詳也。然必曰「緝熈敬止」焉，必曰「敬以勝怠」焉。夫制禮而原於敬，是禮之行於王朝者，不惟其文，惟其本。故當其時，有夏修和而無偷惰之習，四海永清而無僭忒之非。胡氏謂太和在成周宇宙間，盖成周之太和，亦致之以禮讓而已矣。夫何周衰而降，秦不
translation_en:
…the gentleman distinguishes those above from those below and settles the people’s aspirations. And when we read the Analects of Lu, it says: “If one can govern a state through ritual propriety and deference, what difficulty is there? If one cannot govern a state through ritual propriety and deference, what can one do with ritual?” Since settling the people’s aspirations depends upon establishing rites to distinguish those above from those below, the outward forms of ritual establish boundaries for all under Heaven: they must be made clear. Yet since the good government of a state depends upon ritual propriety and deference, the foundations of ritual are especially what accomplish the moral transformation of all under Heaven: they must be honored. Thus, in the age of Tang and Yu, as recorded in the Two Canons, there were pitch standards, measures of length and capacity, and weights; the seasons were announced and governmental arrangements put in order; rites were regulated “like vessels” [?]. The outward forms of ritual were already manifest. Yet the text invariably speaks of being “truly reverent and capable of deference” and “gentle and reverent, truly sincere.” Establishing rites with reverence as their source meant that ritual as practiced at the emperors’ court rested not merely on its outward forms but on its foundations. Thus, in that age, the common people were transformed, bringing about the beauty of concord; the four quarters followed the ruler’s wishes, with the admirable responsiveness of things stirred by the wind. Master Hu said that supreme harmony filled the universe in the age of Tang and Yu. That supreme harmony was brought about simply through ritual propriety and deference.
By the flourishing age of Cheng Zhou, as recorded in the Rites of Zhou, there were the nine occupations and eight regulations, the five rites and six musical traditions, and the three subjects of instruction and six modes of deportment. The outward forms of ritual were certainly even more detailed. Yet the texts invariably speak of “continuing in brightness and abiding in reverence” and “overcoming indolence through reverence.” Establishing rites with reverence as their source meant that ritual as practiced at the royal court rested not merely on its outward forms but on its foundations. Thus, in that age, the people of the central lands cultivated harmony and had no habits of laxity or indolence; all within the four seas remained peaceful, free from the wrongdoing of usurpation and transgression. Master Hu said that supreme harmony filled the universe in the age of Cheng Zhou. That supreme harmony, too, was brought about simply through ritual propriety and deference. How was it, then, that after the decline of Zhou, Qin did not…

title: 隆慶五年進士登科錄
text:
師古而漢稱近古治亦襲秦孝文溺於黃老
未遑禮樂而俗流失世壞敗恬而不知怪也
故賈誼有定經制之請孝宣習於刑名綜核
是務而述舊禮明王制畧而不之講也故王
吉有建萬世長策之議孝元之世朝有變色
之言下有爭闘之患上有自專之士下有不
讓之人治天下者審所上當時固未之審也
故匡衡有不嚴而成化之說大都三臣之言
皆病徒法不足以興治然則欲致太平之治
者其必有得於法之外而後可乎洪惟我
===
太祖高皇帝開天啓運置天下於仁義禮樂之中
建極錫民囿四海於聲名文物之內其以政
防民也如諸司職掌一書大要倣乎周禮表
制參乎輿論舉百官之事括於六卿而綱紀
以明舉六卿之事歸於朝廷而體統以正他
如宮室車輿之等冠冕服飾之差所以別嫌
而明微者靡不嚴且密焉蓋政也莫非禮也
其以禮教民也如
洪武禮制禮儀定式大明集禮諸書其肯斷於
宸衷其書修於曾魯李原名諸臣禮則有吉凶軍

者其必有得於法之外而後可乎洪惟我
===
太祖高皇帝開天啓運混天下於仁義禮樂之中
建極錫民囿四海於聲名文物之内其以政
防民也如諸司職掌一書大要倣乎周禮衷
制參乎輿論舉百官之事括於九卿而綱紀
以明舉九御之事歸於朝廷而禮統以正他
如宫室車輿之等冠冕服飾之差所以别嫌
而明微者靡不嚴且客焉蓋政也莫非禮也
其以禮教民也如
洪武禮制禮儀定式大明集禮諸書其肯斷於
宸衷其書修於曾魯李原名諸臣禮則有吉凶軍
punctuated:
師古，而漢稱近古，治亦襲秦。孝文溺於黃老，未遑禮樂，而俗流失，世壞敗，恬而不知怪也。故賈誼有定經制之請。孝宣習於刑名，綜核是務，而述舊禮、明王制，畧而不之講也。故王吉有建萬世長策之議。孝元之世，朝有變色之言，下有爭闘之患，上有自專之士，下有不讓之人。治天下者審所上，當時固未之審也。故匡衡有不嚴而成化之說。大都三臣之言，皆病徒法不足以興治。然則欲致太平之治者，其必有得於法之外而後可乎？

洪惟我太祖高皇帝開天啓運，置天下於仁義禮樂之中；建極錫民，囿四海於聲名文物之內。其以政防民也，如《諸司職掌》一書，大要倣乎《周禮》，表制參乎輿論。舉百官之事，括於六卿，而綱紀以明；舉六卿之事，歸於朝廷，而體統以正。他如宮室車輿之等，冠冕服飾之差，所以別嫌而明微者，靡不嚴且密焉。蓋政也，莫非禮也。其以禮教民也，如《洪武禮制》《禮儀定式》《大明集禮》諸書，其肯斷於宸衷，其書修於曾魯、李原名諸臣。禮則有吉凶軍
translation_en:
…take antiquity as its model; and although the Han was said to approach antiquity, its government likewise followed the Qin. Emperor Xiaowen was absorbed in the teachings of Huang-Lao and had no time for rites and music. Customs went astray and society deteriorated, yet people complacently found nothing strange in this. Thus Jia Yi petitioned to establish enduring institutions. Emperor Xiaoxuan was practiced in the techniques of assessing performance against assigned responsibilities and devoted himself to comprehensive scrutiny. Yet he neglected to discuss transmitting the ancient rites and elucidating the institutions of the sage kings. Thus Wang Ji proposed establishing a lasting policy for ten thousand generations. In Emperor Xiaoyuan’s time, words spoken at court caused faces to change color in anger, while below there was the scourge of contention and fighting. Above were men who acted on their own authority; below were people unwilling to yield. Those who govern All under Heaven must scrutinize what they exalt, but at that time this had certainly not been scrutinized. Thus Kuang Heng spoke of achieving moral transformation without severity. Broadly speaking, all three ministers’ statements identified the inadequacy of laws alone to bring about good government. Must those who wish to achieve an age of great peace, then, attain something beyond laws before they can succeed?

We reverently reflect that our Emperor Taizu Gao inaugurated a new era and opened the dynasty’s destined rule, placing All under Heaven within benevolence, righteousness, rites, and music. He established the supreme standard and bestowed it upon the people, embracing all within the Four Seas in the forms and institutions of civilization. As for his use of government to restrain the people, the book Duties of the Various Offices broadly followed the Rites of Zhou, consulting public opinion in setting forth its institutions. The affairs of all officials were brought together under the Six Ministers, making the governing framework clear; the affairs of the Six Ministers were referred to the imperial court, setting the hierarchy of authority in order. Other provisions, such as distinctions of rank in palaces, residences, and carriages, and differences in ceremonial headgear and dress, served to distinguish potentially ambiguous cases and clarify subtle distinctions. All were strict and meticulous. These were measures of government, yet none was other than ritual.

As for his use of ritual to instruct the people, there were such books as the Hongwu Ritual Institutions, the Established Forms of Ritual and Ceremony, and the Collected Rites of the Great Ming. Their decisions were made in the imperial mind [?], and the books were compiled by such ministers as Zeng Lu and Li Yuanming. As for rites, there were the auspicious, mourning, military…

title: 隆慶五年進士登科錄
text:
賓嘉之五禮而中正以節樂則有本太初至
樂清寧之九章而和平以宣他如朝叅宴享
之儀儀仗鹵簿之制靡不詳且備焉蓋禮也
莫非政也合文質而兼舉通政教而並行我
高皇帝之制誠為盡美盡善
聖子神孫率而由之信可以致治如唐虞成周之
太和而陋漢之治於不足言也臣伏讀
聖制乃今治績罔效風教未孚而其故由於政之
文徒具禮之實未至是有意於復
高皇之彜典黜今時之靡文所謂明禮之文而必
===
崇禮之本者
聖心既獨得而切思之矣臣敢不為
陛下悉陳之乎大抵天下之勢恒起於尚質而日
趨於尚文國家之治恒始於質勝而日敝於
文勝故孔子於周室之禮樂必從先進而不
從後進焉蓋欲挽文而趨於質撥亂而反之
治此其所以不從彼而從此也我
高皇帝之制禮固
昭代之所謂先進而臣民之所當率從者也夫
何世變日下而人心失真君子長者之道浸

punctuated:
賓、嘉之五禮，而中正以節；樂則有本太初至樂清寧之九章，而和平以宣。他如朝叅宴享之儀、儀仗鹵簿之制，靡不詳且備焉。蓋禮也，莫非政也。合文質而兼舉，通政教而並行，我高皇帝之制誠為盡美盡善。聖子神孫率而由之，信可以致治如唐虞成周之太和，而陋漢之治於不足言也。
臣伏讀聖制，乃今治績罔效，風教未孚，而其故由於政之文徒具、禮之實未至，是有意於復高皇之彜典、黜今時之靡文。所謂明禮之文而必崇禮之本者，聖心既獨得而切思之矣。臣敢不為陛下悉陳之乎？
大抵天下之勢恒起於尚質而日趨於尚文，國家之治恒始於質勝而日敝於文勝。故孔子於周室之禮樂，必從先進而不從後進焉。蓋欲挽文而趨於質，撥亂而反之治，此其所以不從彼而從此也。我高皇帝之制禮，固昭代之所謂先進，而臣民之所當率從者也。夫何世變日下而人心失真，君子長者之道浸
translation_en:
…reception and auspicious ceremonies, completing the five categories of rites, regulated through balance and rectitude. As for music, there are nine movements, from “Rooted in the Great Beginning” (Ben Taichu) to “Music of Purity and Tranquility” (Le Qingning), through which harmony and peace are expressed. Other provisions, such as the ceremonies for court audiences and banquets, and the regulations for ceremonial guards and imperial processions, are all detailed and comprehensive. Thus, nothing in ritual is outside governance. Combining outward refinement with inner substance, and advancing governance together with moral instruction, the institutions of our Emperor Gao are truly perfect in both beauty and goodness. If his sagely sons and divine grandsons follow them, they can assuredly achieve the supreme harmony of the ages of Tang Yao, Yu Shun, and the established Zhou, making the governance of the Han seem so inferior as to be unworthy of mention.
Your servant has reverently read Your Majesty’s decree: at present, government has produced no effective results, and moral instruction has not won the people’s trust. The reason lies in possessing only the outward forms of governance without fully realizing the substance of ritual. Thus, Your Majesty intends to restore Emperor Gao’s enduring institutions and reject the empty elaboration of the present age. As for what is meant by clarifying the forms of ritual while necessarily honoring its foundations, Your Majesty’s sagely mind has already independently grasped this and pondered it earnestly. Dare your servant fail to set it all forth before Your Majesty?
In general, the course of affairs under Heaven always begins with valuing substance and moves daily toward valuing outward refinement. The governance of a state always begins with substance predominating and deteriorates day by day as outward refinement gains the upper hand. Thus, in matters of the Zhou dynasty’s rites and music, Confucius insisted on following the earlier practitioners rather than the later ones. His intention was to turn people back from outward refinement toward substance, to dispel disorder and restore good governance. This is why he followed the former rather than the latter. Our Emperor Gao’s establishment of ritual assuredly represents what may be called the practice of the earlier generation of this illustrious dynasty, which officials and people alike ought to follow. Why, then, have changing times brought daily decline, and why have people’s hearts lost their sincerity, while the way of gentlemen and venerable elders gradually…

title: 隆慶五年進士登科錄
text:
流於虚浮淳龐敦慤之風漸歸於詐偽
國初之民俗至儉約也迨於今而侈泰以相炫
程子所謂農工商賈日志於富侈不能無矣
國初之士習至雅馴也迨於今而睢恣以陵上
程子所謂士大夫日志於尊榮不能無矣以
今而較諸昔彼卿大夫和於朝士庶人和於
野師師濟濟皥皥熈熈以成大猷之治者今
豈能與之髣髴哉盖昔之為禮也有本而後
有文天下舉相率而從其本此唐虞成周之
所以為太和也
===
高皇帝之所以同符虞周之世也今之為禮也有
文而無其本天下舉相率而入於文此西漢
諸臣之所為慨歎也
今日所以當復
高皇帝之治也臣伏讀
聖制終篇曰今欲興教化厚風俗使天下志慮不
易視聽純一相安於蕩蕩平平之治禮讓之
風媲美成周必何施而後可夫教化國家之
急務也而俗吏慢之風俗天下之大事也而
世主忽之其沿襲之弊非一日矣

有文天下皐相率而從其本此唐虞成周之
所以爲太和也
===

今日所以當復
高皇帝之治也臣伏讀
聖制終篇曰今欲興敎化厚風俗使天下志慮不

急務也而俗吏慢之風俗天下之大事也而
世主忽之其沿襲之弊非一日矣
punctuated:
流於虚浮，淳龐敦慤之風漸歸於詐偽。
國初之民俗至儉約也，迨於今而侈泰以相炫，程子所謂「農工商賈日志於富侈」，不能無矣。國初之士習至雅馴也，迨於今而睢恣以陵上，程子所謂「士大夫日志於尊榮」，不能無矣。以今而較諸昔，彼卿大夫和於朝，士庶人和於野，師師濟濟，皥皥熈熈，以成大猷之治者，今豈能與之髣髴哉？盖昔之為禮也，有本而後有文，天下舉相率而從其本，此唐虞成周之所以為太和也，高皇帝之所以同符虞周之世也。今之為禮也，有文而無其本，天下舉相率而入於文，此西漢諸臣之所為慨歎也，今日所以當復高皇帝之治也。
臣伏讀聖制終篇曰：「今欲興教化，厚風俗，使天下志慮不易，視聽純一，相安於蕩蕩平平之治，禮讓之風媲美成周，必何施而後可？」夫教化，國家之急務也，而俗吏慢之；風俗，天下之大事也，而世主忽之。其沿襲之弊，非一日矣。
translation_en:
…degenerates into hollowness and superficiality, while the spirit of simple integrity and earnest sincerity gradually gives way to deception and falsehood.
At the founding of the dynasty, the customs of the people were exceedingly frugal. By now, however, people vie with one another in displays of extravagance. What Master Cheng described as “farmers, artisans, and merchants daily setting their hearts on wealth and luxury” has inevitably appeared. At the founding of the dynasty, the habits of scholars were exceedingly refined and orderly. By now, however, they behave wantonly and defy their superiors. What Master Cheng described as “scholar-officials daily setting their hearts on eminence and glory” has inevitably appeared. If we compare the present with the past, when ministers and grandees lived in harmony at court, and scholars and commoners lived in harmony beyond it, all emulating one another in dignified concord, generous contentment, and happiness, thereby bringing the great Way to fruition in government—can the present even remotely resemble that? In former times, the practice of ritual had its foundation first, and only then its outward forms. All under Heaven led one another in following that foundation. This was how the ages of Tang and Yu and the established Zhou attained supreme harmony, and how Emperor Gao matched the ages of Yu and Zhou. Today, the practice of ritual has outward forms but lacks its foundation, and all under Heaven lead one another into mere form. This is what the ministers of the Western Han lamented, and why we must now restore the governance of Emperor Gao.
Your servant has reverently read the conclusion of Your Majesty’s composition: “We now wish to promote moral instruction and enrich social customs, so that the aims and thoughts of all under Heaven do not waver, and what they look upon and listen to is pure and undivided; so that they may live together peacefully under broad and equitable governance, and their spirit of ritual propriety and deference may rival that of the established Zhou. What measures must be undertaken to achieve this?” Moral instruction is an urgent task of the state, yet commonplace officials slight it. Social customs are a matter of great consequence to all under Heaven, yet rulers neglect them. The harm caused by perpetuating these habits has persisted for far longer than a single day.

title: 隆慶五年進士登科錄
text:
陛下之言及此宗社生靈久安長治之計也臣竊
以為朝廷有教化而後天下有風俗而教化
之所以振舉風俗之所以轉移則在乎禮讓
而已矣今夫卿大夫者教化之所繇興廢者
也卿大夫而不以禮讓相與焉此教化之窒
而不行也必也同寅協恭而有和衷之雅推
賢讓能而無娟嫉之私為大臣而論道經邦
則各竭其誠各輸其悃如詩之碩膚几几可
也為小臣而奔走執事則各分其猷各宣其
力如易之匪躬蹇蹇可也卿大夫咸若是則

Your Majesty’s words on this matter constitute a plan for the enduring peace and lasting order of the dynastic ancestral temples, the altars of soil and grain, and all your living subjects. Your servant humbly believes that only when the court provides moral instruction can proper customs prevail throughout the realm. What invigorates moral instruction and transforms customs is simply ritual propriety and deference. Ministers and grandees determine whether moral instruction flourishes or declines. If they do not treat one another with propriety and deference, moral instruction is obstructed and cannot take effect. They must unite in reverent service, displaying the refinement of harmonious purpose; they must promote the worthy and yield to the capable, harboring no selfish jealousy [?]. As high ministers who deliberate on the Way and order the realm, they should each devote their utmost sincerity and offer their heartfelt loyalty, exemplifying the Book of Odes’ words, “Great in merit, dignified in bearing.” As lesser officials who hasten about their duties, they should each contribute their counsel and exert their strength, exemplifying the Book of Changes’ words, “Beset by difficulties, yet not for their own persons’ sake.” If all ministers and grandees act thus, moral transformation will spread among those above. Would they not rival in excellence Ji and Shao and the assembled lords of the Zhou, who exchanged bows and courtesies at court?

Scholars and commoners determine whether customs rise or deteriorate. If they do not treat one another with propriety and deference, customs drift astray without returning. They must strengthen the foundations and attend to substance, practicing the restraint taught in “The Cricket”; they must esteem refinement and reject frivolity, avoiding the extravagance depicted in “The Mayfly.” Those who pursue learning should unite their aspirations and follow a common direction, cultivating the Way through shared methods, without boasting of their accomplishments. Those who work in the fields [?] should help one another keep watch and guard, and aid one another in times of need, without pursuing their livelihoods solely for their own enrichment. If scholars and commoners all act thus, customs will become fine among those below. Would they not equal in excellence the households of Zhou’s neighborhood and community groupings—bi, lü, zu, and dang—who exchanged bows and courtesies in the countryside? title: 隆慶五年進士登科錄
text:
失德則民無爭心其相須之機固如此也然
猶未也四方之習尚惟繫於
元后之率先臣民之隆汙寔始於
君身之作則
陛下誠欲教化之興而風俗之厚亦惟自上為之
率作乎使上無以率作之而徒責望於下是
猶表之弗正而求其景之直源之弗澄而求
其流之清臣知其弗能也伏惟
陛下端拱穆清之上而豫養乎無體之禮基命宥
密之天而允植乎制作之原如堯舜之允恭
===
===
温恭如文武之敬止敬勝如我
高皇帝之存心省躬敬
天勤民由是禮讓之本端於上而禮教之文敷於
下由是天下之防立於上而天下之化成於
下蓋心和則氣和氣和則形和形和則聲和
聲和則天地之和應故陰陽調風雨時甘露
降五穀登六畜蕃嘉禾興朱草生山不童澤
不涸此和之至也而唐虞成周太和之宇宙
寧不為
陛下之宇宙乎

降五穀登六畜蕃嘉禾興朱草生山不童澤
