陛下之宇宙乎
punctuated:
失德，則民無爭心。其相須之機，固如此也。然猶未也，四方之習尚，惟繫於元后之率先；臣民之隆汙，寔始於君身之作則。陛下誠欲教化之興而風俗之厚，亦惟自上為之率作乎！使上無以率作之，而徒責望於下，是猶表之弗正而求其景之直，源之弗澄而求其流之清，臣知其弗能也。

伏惟陛下端拱穆清之上，而豫養乎無體之禮；基命宥密之天，而允植乎制作之原。如堯舜之允恭温恭，如文武之敬止敬勝，如我高皇帝之存心省躬、敬天勤民。由是禮讓之本端於上，而禮教之文敷於下；由是天下之防立於上，而天下之化成於下。蓋心和則氣和，氣和則形和，形和則聲和，聲和則天地之和應。故陰陽調，風雨時，甘露降，五穀登，六畜蕃，嘉禾興，朱草生，山不童，澤不涸，此和之至也。而唐虞成周太和之宇宙，寧不為陛下之宇宙乎？
translation_en:
…if officials commit no failures of virtue, the people will have no contentious impulses. Such indeed is the mechanism by which these things depend upon one another. Yet this is not all. The customs and preferences of every region depend solely upon the sovereign’s taking the lead; the elevation or degradation of officials and people truly begins with the ruler’s setting a personal example. If Your Majesty truly desires the flourishing of moral instruction and the deepening of good customs, surely you must take the lead from above! If those above fail to provide such leadership and merely place demands and expectations upon those below, this is like seeking a straight shadow from a crooked gnomon, or a clear stream from a turbid source. Your servant knows that this cannot succeed.

I humbly hope that Your Majesty, sitting upright with folded hands in the august purity of your court, will nurture in advance the rites that have no outward form; that, grounding the Mandate in the capacious and profound realm of Heaven [?], you will firmly establish the source of ritual institutions. Emulate the sincere reverence and gentle reverence of Yao and Shun, the abiding reverence and reverence that overcomes other impulses of Kings Wen and Wu, and the preservation of the moral mind, self-examination, reverence for Heaven, and diligent care for the people of our Emperor Gao. Thus the root of ritual propriety and deference will be set right above, and the forms of ritual instruction will spread below; thus safeguards for all under Heaven will be established above, and the moral transformation of all under Heaven will be accomplished below. For when the heart is harmonious, the vital energies are harmonious; when the vital energies are harmonious, the bodily form is harmonious; when the bodily form is harmonious, the voice is harmonious; and when the voice is harmonious, the harmony of Heaven and Earth responds. Thus yin and yang are balanced, wind and rain arrive in season, sweet dew descends, the five grains ripen, the six domestic animals multiply, auspicious grain flourishes, vermilion plants grow, mountains are not bare, and marshes do not dry up. This is harmony at its utmost. Could the world of supreme harmony under Tang Yao, Yu Shun, and the flourishing Zhou then fail to become Your Majesty’s world?

title: 隆慶五年進士登科錄
text:
高皇帝萬世太平之功業寧不為
陛下之功業乎昔董仲舒告武帝曰漢宜損周之
文致用夏之忠言太和之治尚質不尚文也
曰人君正心以正朝廷正百官正萬民而遠
近莫敢不壹於正言導和之本在上不在下
也而又終之曰尊所聞行所知惟加之意而
已言端本之功貴行不貴言也願
陛下於仲舒之言加之意焉臣愚幸甚天下幸甚
臣冒
天威不勝戰慄隕越之至臣謹對

干冒
天威不勝戰慄殞越之至臣謹對
punctuated: 高皇帝萬世太平之功業，寧不為陛下之功業乎？昔董仲舒告武帝曰：「漢宜損周之文，致用夏之忠。」言太和之治尚質不尚文也。曰：「人君正心以正朝廷，正百官，正萬民，而遠近莫敢不壹於正。」言導和之本在上不在下也。而又終之曰：「尊所聞，行所知，惟加之意而已。」言端本之功貴行不貴言也。願陛下於仲舒之言加之意焉！臣愚幸甚，天下幸甚！臣冒天威，不勝戰慄隕越之至。臣謹對。
translation_en: Could Emperor Gao’s achievement of securing enduring peace for ten thousand generations not also become Your Majesty’s achievement? In former times, Dong Zhongshu told Emperor Wu: “The Han should reduce the elaborate forms of the Zhou and put into practice the sincerity of the Xia.” He meant that government fostering supreme harmony values substance over outward refinement. He also said: “The ruler rectifies his heart in order to rectify the court, the hundred officials, and the myriad people, so that none, near or far, dares fail to unite in rectitude.” He meant that the foundation for fostering harmony lies above, not below. He concluded by saying: “Honor what you have heard and practice what you know; only give these your attention.” He meant that the work of setting the foundation aright values action over words. May Your Majesty give heed to Zhongshu’s words! This would be the greatest good fortune for your foolish servant, and the greatest good fortune for all under Heaven! Having presumed upon Your Majesty’s heavenly majesty, your servant trembles with fear, overwhelmed to the point of collapse. Your servant respectfully submits this reply.

title: 隆慶五年進士登科錄
text:
臣鄧以讚
臣對臣聞帝王之御極也有整齊天下之大
法則其趨一有感孚天下之實心則其應神
法者天下之所為依據者也民生有欲而易
流人情無制則易肆若非整頓其法而明示
以收斂約束之意則耳惑于聞目惑于見固
有昧於持循而莫措者矣將何以一其趨心
者天下之所為信從者也小民可親不可愚
常情從好不從令若非純一其心而默運夫
精神意氣之感則告之若罔聞示之若罔見
===
固有習於虛文而無實者矣抑將何以神其
應故帝王之有施於天下也欲其如此則明
示其勿如彼條其紀綱而整頓之取其禮度
而修明之而或繼世承敝之後則又為民申
飭而不倦是則可謂有治法矣既行法於天
下也欲下如此則上亦勿如彼以正而自淑
以禮而自治而或治績罔效之餘則又益自
振勵而不怠是則可謂能正心矣夫國而有
法誰敢不法童子持檄而可使聽遐陬聞詔
而可使從若凜然有範圍節制之限而不敢

臣鄧以讚。

臣對：臣聞帝王之御極也，有整齊天下之大法，則其趨一；有感孚天下之實心，則其應神。法者，天下之所為依據者也。民生有欲而易流，人情無制則易肆。若非整頓其法而明示以收斂約束之意，則耳惑于聞，目惑于見，固有昧於持循而莫措者矣。將何以一其趨？心者，天下之所為信從者也。小民可親不可愚，常情從好不從令。若非純一其心而默運夫精神意氣之感，則告之若罔聞，示之若罔見，固有習於虛文而無實者矣。抑將何以神其應？

故帝王之有施於天下也，欲其如此，則明示其勿如彼；條其紀綱而整頓之，取其禮度而修明之。而或繼世承敝之後，則又為民申飭而不倦，是則可謂有治法矣。既行法於天下也，欲下如此，則上亦勿如彼；以正而自淑，以禮而自治。而或治績罔效之餘，則又益自振勵而不怠，是則可謂能正心矣。

夫國而有法，誰敢不法？童子持檄而可使聽，遐陬聞詔而可使從，若凜然有範圍節制之限而不敢
translation_en:
Your servant, Deng Yizan.

Your servant replies: I have heard that when emperors and kings occupy the supreme throne, if they possess great laws for ordering All Under Heaven, the people will be united in their direction; if they possess a sincere heart that moves All Under Heaven and wins its trust, the response will be wondrous. Laws are what all people rely upon. People are born with desires and readily go astray; human feelings, without restraint, readily become unbridled. Unless the ruler puts his laws in order and clearly conveys his intention to restrain and regulate, their ears will be misled by what they hear and their eyes by what they see. There will surely be those who do not understand what to uphold and follow, and who know not how to act. How, then, can their direction be united? The ruler’s heart is what all people trust and follow. The common people may be drawn close, but they cannot be fooled; ordinarily, people follow what their ruler favors, not what he commands. Unless the ruler makes his heart pure and undivided, silently exerting the moving influence of his spirit, intentions, and vital force, people will act as though they have not heard what they are told or seen what they are shown. There will surely be those habituated to empty forms without substance. How, then, can their response be made wondrous?

Thus, when emperors and kings take measures throughout All Under Heaven, if they wish the people to act in this way, they clearly show them that they must not act in that way. They set out and put in order the guiding principles of government, and cultivate and clarify ritual standards. If they succeed to the throne after abuses have accumulated, they tirelessly reiterate these injunctions for the people. This may be called possessing laws for good government. Once they have put laws into effect throughout All Under Heaven, if they wish those below to act in this way, they themselves above must likewise not act in that way. They improve themselves through uprightness and regulate themselves through ritual propriety. If their efforts at government have failed to produce results, they exert themselves still more, without flagging. This may be called being able to rectify the heart.

Now, if a state has laws, who dares not abide by them? Even a boy bearing an official proclamation can secure obedience, and people in distant corners, hearing an imperial edict, can be made to comply. It is as though, in awe, they faced boundaries of regulation and restraint and dared not …

title: 隆慶五年進士登科錄
text:
越何者其法定也君而心正誰敢不正可以
意指而趨可以氣使而至皆油然有懽忻鼓
舞之意而不能違何者其心孚也由是德歸
其厚而澆薄之風息情從其實而虚詐之習
泯豐儉有宜而不相侈尊卑有等而不相踰
朝著有師穆之休閭野有淳龐之俗而天下
咸登諸理矣欽惟
皇帝陛下秉神聖之資
撫靈長之運百姓既漸乂安四夷皆已稱貢兹
進臣等於
===
廷俯
賜清問惓惓以治績之未效禮法之失實為言
則求治無巳之盛心也臣思是舉也三載一
行相沿為故事然臣伏讀
聖制終篇曰將採而行焉則豈以為故事巳耶臣
敢述所聞以對臣聞之孔子曰政者正也子
產曰禮者民之行也皆言法之當立也故善
理家者必立為家法畫一可守然後親疎大
小皆秩然整肅惟吾之聽而不敢有自異之
心則以家視天下者又可知矣後之論者曰

撫盈長之運百姓既漸乂安四夷皆已稱貢茲
進臣等於
===
延俯
賜清問惓惓以治績之未效禮法之失實爲言
則求治無已之盛心也臣思是舉也三載一
行相沿爲故事然臣伏讀
聖制終篇曰將採而行焉則豈以爲故事已耶臣
敢述所聞以對臣聞之孔子曰政者正也子
産曰禮者民之行也皆言法之當立也故善
理家者必立爲家法畫一可守然後親踈大
小皆秩然整肅惟吾之聽而不敢有自異之
心則以家視天下者又可知矣後之論者曰
punctuated:
越。何者？其法定也。君而心正，誰敢不正？可以意指而趨，可以氣使而至，皆油然有懽忻鼓舞之意而不能違。何者？其心孚也。由是德歸其厚，而澆薄之風息；情從其實，而虚詐之習泯；豐儉有宜，而不相侈；尊卑有等，而不相踰；朝著有師穆之休，閭野有淳龐之俗，而天下咸登諸理矣。
欽惟皇帝陛下秉神聖之資，撫靈長之運，百姓既漸乂安，四夷皆已稱貢。兹進臣等於廷，俯賜清問，惓惓以治績之未效、禮法之失實為言，則求治無巳之盛心也。臣思是舉也，三載一行，相沿為故事。然臣伏讀聖制，終篇曰：「將採而行焉。」則豈以為故事巳耶？臣敢述所聞以對。
臣聞之，孔子曰：「政者，正也。」子產曰：「禮者，民之行也。」皆言法之當立也。故善理家者，必立為家法，畫一可守，然後親疎大小皆秩然整肅，惟吾之聽，而不敢有自異之心。則以家視天下者，又可知矣。後之論者曰：
translation_en:
…transgress them. Why is this? Because the laws are settled. When the ruler’s heart is upright, who dares not be upright? A mere indication of his intention can set people moving; the force of his presence can bring them forward. All spontaneously feel joy and encouragement and cannot go against him. Why is this? Because his heart inspires trust. Thus virtue returns to generosity, and the prevailing tendency toward shallowness subsides; feelings accord with sincerity, and habits of deception disappear. Abundance and frugality each find their proper measure, and people do not vie in extravagance. The honored and the humble have their respective ranks and do not encroach upon one another. The court enjoys harmony [?], and villages and countryside possess honest and generous customs. All under Heaven thus attain good order.
I reverently consider that Your Majesty the Emperor possesses a divine and sagely disposition and presides over an auspicious and enduring reign. The common people have gradually attained peace and order, and the peoples of the four quarters have all presented tribute. Now you have summoned us, your servants, to court and graciously bestowed your discerning questions upon us. You speak with earnest concern about the failure of governance to produce results and the loss of substance in ritual and law. This reveals your magnificent resolve never to cease seeking good government. Your servant reflects that this examination is held once every three years and has become an established practice through successive observance. Yet I have respectfully read your sacred decree, which concludes: “I shall adopt and put them into practice.” How, then, could you regard this merely as an established practice? Your servant ventures to recount what he has learned in reply.
Your servant has learned that Confucius said: “To govern is to rectify.” Zichan said: “Ritual is the conduct of the people.” Both statements mean that laws must be established. Thus one who manages a household well must establish household rules, uniform and capable of being observed. Only then will relatives close and distant, seniors and juniors, all be orderly and disciplined, obeying him alone and daring not entertain any intention of departing from his rules. From this one can also understand how to regard all under Heaven as a household. Later thinkers said: …

title: 隆慶五年進士登科錄
text:
焚符破璽而民朴鄙剖斗折衡而民不爭曰
禮者忠信之薄而亂之首是謂卧而治之遂
可以宰制宇内矣夫風氣漸漓人心反古以
今日而欲為太古之無事是猶太冬之候責
裘者以為葛之易也豈不謬哉又聞之蔡沈
曰典章文物心之著也禮樂教化心之發也
皆言心之當正也故善治身者必内定其心
常惺常覺而能為四體之主則凡意有所向
手持足行皆將不待使令而率然以自至則
以身視天下者又可知矣後之論者曰鞭朴
===
不可弛於家刑罰不可廢於國曰殺一人刑
二人而天下治蓋謂刑以繩之遂可以震懾
宇内矣夫上有所好下必甚焉不自治而欲
為申韓之酷法是猶立枉木而求影之直也
豈可得哉故禮有符契所以養信也上好權
謀則下將乗是而為欺禮有命討所以明公
也上好枉曲則下將借是而為私車服有章
禮之飾也上務觀美則下將侈靡以相競交
際不諂禮之節也上務簡忽則下將傲惰以
相高故曰徒善不足以為政徒法不能以自

translation_en:
…“Burn the tallies and break the seals, and the people will become simple and rustic; split the grain measures and snap the balance beams, and the people will cease to contend.” They also said: “Ritual is the attenuation of loyalty and trustworthiness, and the beginning of disorder.” This means, they supposed, that one could govern reclining at ease and thereby command all within the realm. Yet prevailing customs have gradually deteriorated, and people’s hearts have turned away from antiquity [?]. To seek the untroubled condition of remotest antiquity in the present day is like, in the depths of winter, reproaching someone wearing furs on the grounds that wearing hemp cloth would be easier [?]. Is this not misguided?

I have also heard these words of Cai Shen: “Institutions and cultural forms are the manifestations of the heart; ritual, music, instruction, and moral transformation are its expressions.” These all speak of the need to rectify the heart. Thus, one skilled in governing himself must first bring stability to his heart within, keeping it constantly alert and aware, so that it can serve as master of the four limbs. Then, wherever his intention turns, whatever his hands hold and wherever his feet go, all will follow spontaneously without awaiting commands. From this, too, one can understand how to regard the governance of the realm through the example of governing oneself.

Later commentators said: “The whip and rod cannot be dispensed with in the household, nor punishments abolished in the state.” They also said: “Execute one person and punish two, and the realm will be well governed.” They supposed that by restraining people through punishment, one could overawe all within the realm. Yet whatever those above favor, those below will pursue still more intensely. To fail to govern oneself while wishing to implement the harsh laws of Shen and Han is like setting up a crooked piece of wood and expecting its shadow to be straight. How could this be achieved?

Thus ritual provides tallies and contracts to nurture trustworthiness; but if those above delight in expedient schemes, those below will exploit these instruments to practice deceit. Ritual provides commands for punitive action to make impartial justice manifest; but if those above delight in perverting what is right, those below will use these commands to serve private interests. Carriages and robes have prescribed distinctions: these are ritual’s outward adornments. But if those above devote themselves to splendid appearances, those below will compete in extravagance. Social dealings without flattery express ritual’s measured restraint; but if those above devote themselves to casual neglect, those below will vie in arrogance and indolence. Thus it is said: “Good intentions alone are insufficient for governing, and laws alone cannot of themselves …

title: 隆慶五年進士登科錄
text:
行信乎心與法之當兼也昔黃帝
自正虞舜無為而天下治其風不
代以来惟周獨盛今觀周禮也有
萬民有八則以治都鄙其條已具
五禮以節之六樂以和之三物以
以稽之其所彰軌物而示之趨者
也故凡言治者莫不曰周官之法
公也皆從廣大心中流出皆從天
作之已非苟矣而頌君德者曰純
曰敬義以自持曰基命宥密曰對
===
所以植本原而示之極者又無不
稱治者亦莫不曰關雎麟趾之意
而民不敢犯心運而民自樂從往
犯難則忘危以尊臨者授之事而
卑事者服其事而不言勞至于數
于興師猶有與子同袍之盟彼豈
能作其勤事之氣耶莫不欲富而
以自侈莫不欲尊而不敢越分以
結者不知冠冕之為華食藜藿者
之為美至于數十世而顧瞻周道

之為美至于數十世而顧瞻周道
punctuated: 行。信乎，心與法之當兼也！昔黃帝自正，虞舜無為而天下治，其風不代以来，惟周獨盛。今觀周禮也，有萬民，有八則以治都鄙，其條已具。五禮以節之，六樂以和之，三物以以稽之，其所彰軌物而示之趨者也。故凡言治者，莫不曰周官之法，公也。皆從廣大心中流出，皆從天作之，已非苟矣。而頌君德者，曰「純」，曰「敬義以自持」，曰「基命宥密」，曰「對」。所以植本原而示之極者，又無不稱治者，亦莫不曰《關雎》《麟趾》之意。而民不敢犯，心運而民自樂從。往犯難則忘危，以尊臨者授之事，而卑事者服其事而不言勞。至于數于興師，猶有與子同袍之盟。彼豈能作其勤事之氣耶？莫不欲富，而以自侈；莫不欲尊，而不敢越分。以結者不知冠冕之為華，食藜藿者之為美。至于數十世，而顧瞻周道。
translation_en: …operate. Truly, the heart and laws must both be employed! In former times, the Yellow Emperor rectified himself, and Yu Shun practiced nonaction, yet All under Heaven was well governed. Their influence did not…; since the … dynasties [?], Zhou alone flourished. Now, examining the Rites of Zhou, we find … the myriad people [?], and eight regulations for governing the metropolitan and outlying domains; its provisions were already complete. The five rites regulated them, the six musical traditions harmonized them, and the three subjects … examined them [?]. These were the means by which it displayed proper standards and showed people the direction to follow. Thus, all who discuss government speak of the laws of the Offices of Zhou … impartiality [?]. All flowed from a broad and capacious heart; all proceeded from Heaven … their establishment was certainly no casual undertaking [?]. Those who praised the ruler’s virtue said, “Pure …”; “Maintain oneself through reverence and righteousness”; “The founding mandate was magnanimous and tranquil”; and “Facing …” [?]. These were the means by which the roots were established and the highest standard displayed … [?]. All who praise good government likewise speak of the meaning of “The Ospreys Cry” (Guanju) and “The Qilin’s Hoofs” (Linzhi). … And the people dared not transgress; the heart acted, and the people gladly followed of themselves. Going forth to confront difficulties, they forgot danger. Those who presided from a position of honor assigned tasks, while those serving in humble positions performed their duties without complaining of toil. Even when … troops were raised [?], there remained the pledge, “With you I share my robe.” Could they … rouse their spirit of diligent service [?]? None did not desire wealth, yet … indulged themselves in extravagance [?]; none did not desire honor, yet they dared not overstep their allotted station. Those … with knots [?] did not regard official caps as splendid; those who ate goosefoot and bean leaves … as delicious [?]. Even after several tens of generations, they looked back toward the way of Zhou …
